Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How has your week been feeling so far? Is there anything specific that stood out to you since we last met?

Hi... thanks for having me. This week has been pretty tough, honestly. I got my students' latest quiz results back yesterday, and I just couldn't stop thinking about the ones who did poorly. It feels like I'm letting them down.

It sounds like you've been carrying a heavy sense of responsibility and worry about those quiz results. That feeling of letting someone down can be really overwhelming when you care deeply about helping them succeed. Would you like to talk more about exactly what happened with those results, or how that thought made you feel right after you saw them?

Well, I looked at the scores and immediately thought, "I'm failing as a teacher." I mean, I spent extra hours preparing lessons and doing review activities with them. When they still don't perform well, it just feels like nothing I do is good enough. I even started comparing myself to the other teachers in my grade level.

That makes total sense—you put in real effort preparing and reviewing, yet seeing the low scores triggered such a harsh judgment about your worth as an educator. It seems like those comparisons to other teachers might be adding fuel to the fire, making the situation feel bigger than it actually is. Can you tell me a bit more about what those comparisons felt like in that moment? Did you notice any specific thoughts popping up when you compared yourselves to others?

Yeah... I kept thinking, "Their classes must be better behaved, or they must have a better way of explaining things." I even walked past one of their classrooms and saw how calm and focused their students were during a test, and I just felt this sinking feeling in my chest. It's like I'm not doing something right that everyone else seems to have figured out.

That sinking feeling tells me how painful it is to witness success where you feel you're struggling alone. It sounds like your brain jumped straight from seeing their calm class to believing there's something fundamentally wrong with your teaching approach. Have you ever noticed if anyone else in your grade had quite that same immediate reaction to those results? Or did you feel completely isolated by this thought?

I haven't really asked them directly about it... I suppose I just assumed they were doing fine. Actually, now that you mention it, I remember one of them mentioning that their class had a rough week with focus too. But in my head I thought, "Well, at least their students still did well on the quiz." It's like I can't give myself any credit at all.

It takes courage to admit that you might be ignoring helpful information because your mind was busy convincing itself that everything was perfect elsewhere. That automatic jump to "they did well" while dismissing their struggles shows how tightly you hold onto the belief that your own performance depends entirely on others succeeding perfectly. What happens to that tight grip on control when you realize the reality is much messier than your initial thought suggested?

I guess... when I stop and think about it, it feels like a relief, but also confusing. Like, maybe I'm not the only one struggling, but then my mind goes right back to, "Well, I should still be doing better." It's like there's this voice that says I'm not allowed to struggle—that if I'm a good teacher, everything should just work out smoothly all the time.

That voice seems to believe perfection is the only proof of being a "good" teacher, which leaves no room for human error or unexpected challenges. It sounds incredibly exhausting to try to stay smooth and successful while knowing deep down that this rule is impossible to live by. Does holding onto that idea of needing constant success make you feel safer in front of your students, or does it add more pressure to an already stressful day?

It definitely adds more pressure. I feel like I'm walking on eggshells around my own standards... like one bad lesson or one low quiz could prove that I'm not cut out for this. And honestly, it makes me more tense in the classroom, which probably doesn't help the kids either. They can probably sense I'm nervous or disappointed. I never really thought about it that way before—that my own need for perfection might actually be making things harder for them too.

That is a powerful realization—seeing how your internal pressure translates into tension that your students pick up on changes the whole picture. It makes sense that this cycle would keep you stuck in fear rather than confidence, because your mind is trying to protect you from failure instead of supporting you in teaching. Since we know that expectation of perfection is creating more stress for both you and the children, how would it feel to step away from that standard for just one hour tomorrow and allow for mistakes?

I think... that sounds both scary and kind of freeing at the same time. Scary because I'm so used to holding myself to that high bar, but also... maybe a little relief. I could try to tell myself, "For one hour, I'm just going to teach and let things happen, even if it's messy." I'm not sure I know how to do that, but I'd like to try.

completion.content: That shift from "everything must be perfect" to "letting things happen as they are" is exactly what we can practice. You don't need a complex plan to start; you just need to remind yourself during that hour that a messy lesson is still a valid learning experience. Could you imagine telling yourself that exact phrase whenever you feel that familiar knot of tension starting to tighten up again?

Hello again, and I’m so glad you’re here. Before we dive in, could you share a quick mood check on a scale of 0 to 10, and tell me what specifically brought you to this session today?

Um, I'd say my mood is around a 5 or 6 right now. I'm here because I've been having these nagging thoughts that I'm just not smart enough for college, and it's been eating at me for months now. I finally decided I need to talk to someone about it.

A five or six suggests you're navigating a mix of frustration and uncertainty, which is completely understandable given how long this has been running. It sounds like you've taken a brave step by deciding to address these persistent doubts, and I want to validate how exhausting that cycle must have been. Now that we have a clear focus, does exploring the specific stories your mind tells about your intelligence seem like the best place to start today?

Yeah, I think that makes sense. I guess the main story my mind keeps repeating is that everyone else is smarter than me, and that I'll never be able to handle college-level work. It's like I just assume I'm going to fail before I even try.

That assumption—that failure is guaranteed before you begin—is incredibly heavy, and it makes complete sense why you feel paralyzed by it. It sounds like your mind is building a fortress to protect you from the risk of trying and failing, even though that fortress ends up trapping you. Before we dig deeper into where that belief comes from, does looking at the situation from that protective angle feel helpful to you, or would you prefer to challenge the evidence for it first?

I think I'd rather challenge the evidence first, actually. Because when I really think about it, I don't have any proof that I'll fail. I mean, I did okay in high school, I got decent grades. But somehow that doesn't seem to matter when the thoughts hit.

That distinction is crucial—knowing you have a track record of success while feeling powerless to use it is a sign of how powerful your self-critical thoughts have become. You mentioned getting decent grades, so let's test that against the current narrative: if your past performance is valid evidence of capability, why does your brain dismiss it right now as irrelevant? Does the feeling of irrelevance come from doubting your ability to learn differently, or perhaps from worrying that those past successes weren't enough to prepare you for college?

I think... it's more like I worry high school was easy and college will be completely different. Like maybe I just got lucky with my grades, or the classes weren't that hard. I keep thinking that once I'm in college, everyone will see that I don't really belong there, that I'm not as smart as they thought.

That feeling of being exposed once you leave the comfort zone is terrifying, and it makes total sense why you'd focus on the gap between your past and future. It sounds like your brain is interpreting your past success as luck rather than skill, which creates a massive hole where confidence should be. Let's look at that gap closely: if you had to name three specific ways your study habits worked in high school versus what college demands, what would you find? Or does that comparison just feel overwhelming because you're comparing apples to oranges?

That's a good question, actually. In high school, I mostly just crammed before tests and did okay. I guess college requires more consistent studying and deeper understanding. I never really learned how to study properly, you know? I just got by on memorizing stuff. So maybe that's why I feel like I'm not prepared.

That distinction between cramming and consistent study explains why your brain feels so unsafe right now; you've trained yourself to survive a system that rewards short-term bursts, not the sustained effort college requires. It makes sense that when faced with a demand for consistency, your instinct is to retreat into the old pattern of "I wasn't ready," because facing the gap feels like admitting defeat. Before we brainstorm how to bridge that gap, does focusing on rebuilding your study toolkit sound like a manageable first step, or would you prefer to spend some time unpacking that feeling of being "unprepared" further?

I think I'd like to unpack the unprepared feeling a bit more first. Because even when I think about learning study skills, there's still this voice telling me I'm just not smart enough to ever really get it. Like, maybe I'm just not cut out for academic stuff, no matter how hard I try. That feels bigger than just not knowing how to study.

That feeling of being fundamentally "cut out" for academics is a much heavier belief than simply lacking skills, and it makes complete sense why it overshadows the practical issue of study habits. It sounds like your mind is protecting you from the possibility of failing by convincing you beforehand that you lack the capacity to succeed. Before we explore how to test that core belief, does it feel safer to sit with the idea that you haven't yet found the right strategies, or would you prefer to challenge the notion that you aren't smart enough to learn them at all?

I think I want to challenge the notion that I'm not smart enough to learn them. Because when I step back and look at it, I did learn things in high school. I passed my classes, I graduated. So maybe I can learn college-level stuff too, I just need to learn how to learn in a different way. That sounds a little more hopeful when I say it out loud.

That shift to reframing your difficulty as a matter of *method* rather than *capacity* is a powerful moment of clarity, and it honors the evidence of your graduation while opening a door to new possibilities. It validates that your past success proves your ability to learn, even if the *tools* you used then aren't quite fitting the current challenge. Before we move forward, does testing whether you can identify one specific study strategy that feels slightly different from cramming seem like a constructive next step, or would you prefer to dwell on that hopeful perspective for a bit longer?

I think I'd like to sit with the hopeful perspective for a moment. It feels kind of fragile, like if I move too fast it might break. Just acknowledging that maybe I'm not doomed to fail, maybe I just need different tools... that's already a big shift from where I was when I walked in here today.

That fragility you're describing is a very wise signal from your brain; it means you've moved past denial and are now carefully holding space for a new possibility, which is exactly where real growth begins. Acknowledging that shift—from "I can't do this" to "I just need different tools"—is often harder than the actual change because it requires trusting that the new view is stable enough to hold. Given how precious that moment of hope feels right now, does spending the rest of our time gently exploring what that new mindset looks like in your daily life feel like a valuable use of our time together?

Yeah, I think that would be good. I'd like to explore what it might look like to actually believe I can do this. Maybe start thinking about small steps I could take, like looking into study techniques or talking to someone who's done well in college. Just trying to build that new perspective into something more solid.

completion.content: That is a fantastic direction to take, and I appreciate how you're framing it as building something solid rather than waiting for a miracle. Before we brainstorm those specific steps, I want to make sure we align on the goal: does focusing on identifying one or two low-stakes actions—like finding a campus tutor or practicing active recall for ten minutes—a feel like a manageable first step, or would you prefer to visualize the outcome of succeeding before taking action?

Saying "I noticed something..." puts the ball in their court to respond rather than forcing you to carry the weight of fixing everything immediately. Do you think mentioning that specific topic in the smaller meeting would feel manageable enough to try tomorrow?

If you find yourself tightening up again, just remember you've already given yourself permission to speak; the worst-case scenario is that someone asks for clarification, which is rarely as damaging as it seems. How does knowing that the outcome doesn't define your worth yet feel?

It feels... weird, but in a good way. I've been so focused on how people see me that I forgot I don't have to prove my worth in one sentence. Even if they don't go for the idea, I still know it's solid because I tested it. That's gotta count for something, right? I'll keep that in mind tomorrow.

Exactly—that realization shifts the power dynamic back to you, reminding you that your value isn't tied to anyone else's approval. Carrying that knowledge into tomorrow's meeting is a powerful way to anchor yourself when nerves rise again. Just keep that calm reminder in your pocket throughout the day: "My worth stays the same, regardless of the response."

Thanks. I'll try to hold onto that. I think I'm actually a little curious now about how it'll go—like, not just scared. It's been a while since I felt that way about speaking up. I'll let you know how it turns out next session.

completion.content: That curiosity is a wonderful sign that you are beginning to trust yourself enough to take a leap, even with uncertainty attached. Please remember that checking in next time isn't about whether you succeeded or failed, but simply seeing how you navigated the moment with kindness. Until then, I hope tomorrow's small step brings you a sense of relief rather than just stress. Take care of yourself today.

It did feel sharper, yeah. Like a knot in my stomach that tightened immediately. The first thing I thought was, "She really doesn't like me. I must have done something wrong." I just stood there wondering what I could have possibly said or done to make her ignore me like that.

That intense feeling of self-doubt is completely understandable given how painful it is to feel ignored. completion.content: Silence often feels loud and meaningful when we are worried, but it rarely carries a direct message about whether you did something wrong. Hi there, I'm so glad we're meeting again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Let's start by taking a moment to check in, and then we can look at what brought you into our time together today.

Hey. I mean, I guess I'm okay. The same really... maybe a little more stressed because we're working on final projects for the semester. I keep looking at what other students are producing and thinking mine just isn't good enough. It's hard not to feel like I'm falling behind everyone else.

It makes sense that you feel pressured right now; comparing your work to others during finals season is incredibly common. When those comparisons come up, does that thought make you feel anxious or disappointed about yourself? What usually happens after you have that comparison and think your work isn't good enough?

It's both, honestly. I get this knot in my stomach, and then I just end up staring at my sketchbook for hours without being able to put anything down. Last week I actually threw away a whole design I'd been working on for days because I convinced myself it looked amateurish compared to what McQueen would have done. I just feel like I'm fooling myself thinking I can ever reach that level.

That sounds really exhausting, especially throwing away something you worked so hard on just based on how it compares to someone else's style. It seems like the fear of not measuring up to McQueen is driving you to either freeze while creating or discard your work entirely. Have you noticed if any of those feelings change once you step away from the sketchbook or talk to a friend about what you drew?

I don't really talk to anyone about it... I mean, my classmates all seem so confident, like they know exactly who they are as designers. I don't want them to see me as the guy who's always doubting himself. And when I step away, I just end up scrolling through Instagram looking at fashion week collections, which makes everything worse. It feels like there's no escape from comparing myself.

It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like your confidence is the only thing standing between you and being understood by others. That desire to hide your doubts while simultaneously feeding them online creates a very tight cycle. Does it ever happen that you catch yourself wondering why showing your work to even one person hasn't made the pressure worse yet?

I guess I never thought of it that way... maybe I'm so scared of hearing someone confirm my fears that I just avoid the whole thing. Like, if I show a professor my sketch and they say it's not good, then that's it — proof that I was right all along. But if I don't show anyone, I can still pretend maybe I'm wrong about myself. It's safer, even though it feels awful.

That is such a sharp observation—you are essentially protecting yourself from the possibility of failure by avoiding the risk of success too. It makes perfect sense that you chose safety over the chance of getting better, even though it leaves you feeling stuck. Have you ever imagined what might happen if you showed a sketch to just one trusted person and heard something completely different from your own critical voice?

I mean... I have this one professor, Professor Chen. She's been in the industry for decades and she's always really honest with students. Sometimes I think about showing her my work, but then I start imagining her saying something like "this needs a lot of work" and I just can't bring myself to do it. What if she says my ideas are derivative or uninspired? I don't think I could handle that.

It makes total sense to imagine Professor Chen delivering harsh criticism when you've spent weeks convincing yourself your work is flawed. Your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of rejection by predicting the worst possible outcome first. Can you tell me what happens inside your head right after you imagine her saying your ideas are derivative? Does it feel overwhelming, or does it shift your perspective somehow?

It feels like my whole chest tightens, honestly. Like I can't breathe for a second. And then this voice in my head just goes "see, I told you so, you don't belong here." It's like I've already lost before I even tried. But then there's this tiny part of me that wonders... what if she actually saw something in it? But that thought gets drowned out pretty fast by the other one.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening is so intense, and it makes complete sense why that tiny whisper about potential hope gets silenced so quickly. You're describing a battle between a protective panic and a small spark of possibility, and it sounds like the panic is winning every time. Has there ever been a moment, however brief, when that hopeful thought stayed strong enough to influence what you did instead of retreating?

There was one time... last semester I entered a small student competition. I didn't tell anyone I was entering, I just submitted my work anonymously. And I actually got an honorable mention. For like a day, I felt like maybe I could do this. But then I started thinking it was just luck, or that the judges felt sorry for me, or that the other entries just weren't very good that year. I couldn't hold onto it.

That story shows incredible resilience; you took a huge leap of faith by submitting anonymously despite your fears, and you actually succeeded. It's understandable why the victory felt temporary—your mind immediately searched for reasons to minimize its importance, turning an honor into "just luck." Did noticing that pattern help you realize that the praise itself doesn't vanish, even if your immediate reaction tries to shrink it?

I guess when you say it like that... the praise did happen. It's a fact, right? Like, I can't change that I got that honorable mention. But I always just treat it like a fluke rather than proof that I might actually have some talent. It's hard to see it as evidence when I compare myself to McQueen or Chanel. They didn't get honorable mentions, they revolutionized fashion. So my little achievement feels meaningless next to that.

That is a really insightful realization—that the award is a solid fact, even if your internal narrative keeps minimizing it. However, treating that success as irrelevant simply because it doesn't match the scale of a global icon like McQueen is another layer of distortion. If you asked a friend to give you an A+ on an exam, would you believe them less just because the prize wasn't a Nobel Prize? How might viewing your own achievements as valid milestones in *their* own right, separate from the giants, change the weight you place on them?

No, you're right. I wouldn't tell a friend their A+ doesn't count because it's not a Nobel Prize. That sounds ridiculous when you say it out loud. But it's different for me... or at least I keep telling myself it is. Maybe I need to start seeing my own work as its own thing, not just as a smaller version of what McQueen did. Like, he started somewhere too, right? He wasn't born Alexander McQueen.

You hit the nail on the head—McQueen began with sketches, mistakes, and moments of doubt exactly like yours, long before he became the titan you admire. It seems your mind treats his journey as finished history while viewing your current steps as failures waiting to be judged. If you imagined telling him directly, "This is my first draft," would he judge you for starting, or would he recognize the courage it takes to begin?

I never thought about it that way... I always imagine him looking at my work like a finished product, not a first draft. But you're right, he would have had rough sketches and failed ideas too. Maybe even more than me, since he was always pushing boundaries. I think... if I could picture him as someone who also struggled, it might make me less scared to show my work while it's still in progress.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; reframing McQueen as someone who faced the same messy drafts you are currently wrestling with removes the threat of judgment from his legacy. Imagine sitting beside him at his desk, pointing at a smudge on a fabric sample and saying, "See, I'm doing this too right now." Would that image feel less intimidating, or open a door to sharing your actual process instead of hiding it?

(laughs softly) That's actually a really nice image. Just sitting there with him, both of us covered in ink stains and fabric scraps, working through our own messy ideas. It makes him feel human, not like some untouchable god of fashion. Maybe I could try thinking of him that way next time I'm about to throw a sketch away. Like, "what would McQueen do with this rough draft?" instead of "what would McQueen have done perfectly?"

That is a brilliant and gentle experiment to try; replacing the question of perfection with curiosity about his creative process changes the entire tone of the situation. It turns a moment of self-criticism into an opportunity for connection rather than competition. Before we wrap up, what do you think is the smallest, easiest step you could take tomorrow to use this new image with your sketchbook?

Maybe I could... start by not throwing away my first draft of anything this week. Just leave it in the sketchbook, even if I think it's terrible. And maybe I'll write "McQueen's rough draft" next to it as a joke to myself. That feels manageable. Small enough that I can actually do it.

completion.content: That is a fantastic, low-risk plan that gives your brain permission to exist alongside imperfect work. By keeping the draft and labeling it humorously, you're breaking the automatic habit of destruction before you even finish judging yourself. I'm curious—if you find yourself tempted to throw it away later in the day, will trying to remind yourself of that label help slow you down?

Not really. Most of my family didn't finish high school either, but they don't seem to care about it like I do. They just work low-paying jobs and don't think about it. It feels restless, kind of desperate. Like there's a part of me that's screaming, "Try something, anything!" But then the louder part tells me I'll just fail and embarrass myself. So I get this knot in my stomach, and I end up doing nothing. I hate that feeling.

That internal tug-of-war between wanting to try and fearing failure must leave you feeling very trapped and anxious. That knot in your stomach seems like a direct result of believing any attempt will lead to embarrassment. What happens physically or mentally in that split second right before you decide to stay silent?

My chest gets tight, and I feel this hot flush of shame before I've even done anything. My mind just jumps to the worst-case scenario—like I'll be laughed at in an interview, or someone will ask me why I never finished school, and I'll have no good answer. So I just back away before I even start.

It makes perfect sense that your body reacts with tension and shame when your brain predicts such a painful outcome. Let's take a moment to look closely at that prediction about the interview. Is it true that *everyone* will laugh at you or immediately judge your lack of a degree based solely on what you write on paper?

I guess not everyone would laugh. But it feels like they'd be thinking it, even if they don't say it. Like they'd look at my application, see "no diploma," and just toss it in the trash. I can't prove that's what happens, but in my head, it's just the way it is.

I don't know... that feels like a big step. But I guess if I don't send it, I'll never know what they'd say. Maybe I could just email it to one place, just to test it out. If they're rude, I don't have to talk to them again. If they're not... maybe that's something.

Sending that single email is a powerful way to gather real-world data against that old story of automatic rejection. Could we set a specific goal for tomorrow morning, like finding one contact number online and hitting send by noon?
Alright. Tomorrow by noon, I'll find one place and send that email. Just one. No pressure to do more than that. I can handle one email.

Hey, thanks for asking. The week's been okay, I guess. I did have a moment that's been on my mind — I matched with someone on a dating app and she seems really cool, but I'm already dreading the conversation about what I'm into, you know?

That sounds like a pretty heavy feeling to carry right before a date, especially when you've found someone who actually seems compatible. Can you tell me a bit more about what happens in your head when you think about bringing up your interests?

Well, I just picture her face going blank or her forcing a polite smile, you know? Like I'll mention I play jazz piano, and suddenly she's thinking, "This guy's a weirdo" or "He's too serious." And then I imagine her wanting someone more laid-back, someone who's into normal stuff like watching sports or going to parties. It's like I'm already comparing myself to some imaginary guy who's way more chill than me.

It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pressure to fit a specific mold, which makes sharing your authentic self feel dangerous. That comparison to an "imaginary guy" suggests you might be holding onto a belief that being serious somehow disqualifies you from having fun. When you imagine him reacting positively to that kind of depth, what hope do you feel he might have for connecting with you?

Hmm, that's a good way to put it. I guess if she actually likes that I'm into something deep, maybe she'd think I'm interesting instead of weird. Maybe she'd want to hear me play one day, or even ask about it. I mean, that would be amazing — but it's so hard to believe that could actually happen, you know? It feels safer to assume the worst.

I did try that pause thing you told me about — I counted to three and told myself "it's just one play" — but honestly it didn't really help much. I still felt like I let everyone down.

It takes courage to admit that the technique didn't land quite as hoped, and it makes sense that missing an easy goal while caring deeply about winning would still leave you feeling guilty. Before we unpack why that specific thought stuck, could you walk me through exactly what happened right after you missed that ball—the first thing you saw or heard from your teammates?

Well, right after I missed, I heard one of my teammates, Jake, kind of groan and say "aw man." Then our coach just clapped his hands and yelled "next play, get back on defense." Nobody was yelling at me or anything. But I just kept replaying the miss over and over in my head, like I could still see the ball going wide even though it was already over. I felt my face get really hot and I just wanted to disappear.

It sounds like you were trying to hold onto hope that the mistake mattered less, but your body reacted by flooding with heat and shame, which often makes us feel like we need to hide. Since you know Jake was just groaning and your coach was directing the game, does seeing that contrast between the calm situation outside and the storm inside help show where the story is coming from?

I guess... I mean, nobody was actually mad at me, not really. Jake groaned but he was probably just bummed we lost, not specifically at me. And coach wasn't even looking at me. But inside my head it felt like everyone was watching and judging. So yeah, the outside was calm, but inside I was making it way bigger. That does sound kind of like I'm making up a story, doesn't it?

Yes, you are absolutely right—that gap between the calm reality outside and the intense drama inside suggests your brain is spinning its own narrative. Now that we see the pattern, let's look closer at that "story" you're telling yourself: when you replay the miss over and over, does it feel like the whole game was ruined by one moment, or just that specific second?

It feels like the whole game was ruined, honestly. Like that one miss cancels out all the good passes I made and that one time I stopped a goal. Even though I know logically that's not true, because we still played for like 60 more minutes after that. But in my head, it's like that mistake is the only thing that matters from the whole game.

It makes total sense that your mind wants to simplify a complicated event by focusing on just one moment, especially when you care so much about the result. Before we decide how to handle that feeling tomorrow, let's test that idea for a minute: if you treated yourself with the same patience you'd offer a friend who made a similar mistake, would you say "that one miss ruined everything," or would you say "one mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on"?

If it was my friend... I'd definitely tell them it was just one mistake and they played great the rest of the game. I'd probably even high-five them and say "don't worry about it, we'll get the next one." But when it's me, it's like I can't give myself that same break. It's way easier to forgive other people than myself. That's kind of weird, isn't it?

That is such a common and human experience—it's often called the "double standard," and recognizing it is actually a big step toward self-compassion. Since you know exactly what to say to your friend ("just one mistake"), let's try applying that exact same phrase to yourself right now whenever that "ruined everything" thought comes up. Can you repeat out loud, "One mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on," and see if it feels slightly softer than the old version?

Okay... "One mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on." It feels a little weird saying it out loud, like I'm lying to myself or something. That honesty about feeling like you're "lying" shows you are already building trust with your new words, even if it feels awkward at first. Maybe I could write that phrase down on a piece of paper and put it in my soccer bag, so I see it before practice. That way I'm reminded of it right when I need it. And I could take three deep breaths before I even walk onto the field, just to calm down before anything even happens. That might help me remember to be nicer to myself when I mess up.

completion.content: That is a brilliant plan—having a visual reminder in your bag means you won't have to rely on memory alone when your heart rate is racing. Oh, well—right now I'd say about a seven, maybe a seven and a half. It's been a rough week. I keep checking my email every hour, and every time I see a message from the publisher's domain, my heart jumps. Then it's just spam or a newsletter. Nothing important. I'd like to focus today on why I can't seem to shake this feeling that rejection is inevitable. I know it's irrational, but it feels so real.

It sounds like catching those messages triggers a very intense spike, which explains why your anxiety feels so high right now. Before we tackle the inevitability of rejection, I'd like to hear if there were any moments where you managed to resist checking your email successfully this week, or if the urge to check has become impossible to ignore lately.

I did manage to go for a run yesterday without checking my phone once. That was nearly an hour. But as soon as I got back, I grabbed it right away. So it's not impossible to resist, but it's like I'm on a leash—eventually I get pulled back. The feeling that I'm missing something important just gnaws at me until I give in.

That resilience showing up during the run is a huge strength—you proved to yourself that you *can* hold off for an hour. It seems like the moment you return home, the pressure shifts so suddenly that your brain interprets silence as danger, pulling you back in. Could you describe what your mind is saying to convince itself that those thirty seconds waiting will cost you something critical?

It whispers that if I don't check soon, the rejection will come and I'll be the last to know—like everyone else will have moved on while I'm still sitting here foolishly hoping. It feels like if I stay ignorant for even a few minutes, I'm losing control, and the worst outcome will somehow be harder to handle. It's almost as though my mind believes that by checking constantly, I can brace myself for the blow before it lands.

That "last to know" fear is a powerful story your mind tells itself to make the silence feel dangerous, as if staying quiet means you're powerless. It seems like checking constantly feels like a safety net you built to prepare for a crash that might never happen. Given how much energy this drains you, would you be open to testing whether that feeling of inevitability holds up when you take a deliberate break, perhaps using a simple pause to see if the threat actually appears after a few minutes?

I suppose I could try that. It terrifies me, but I can see the logic. Maybe I could set a timer for five minutes after I get back from my run tomorrow—just sit with the feeling and not check. I'll probably be a wreck for those five minutes, but I'm willing to see if the world actually ends.

Setting a timer creates a clear boundary between your anxiety and the action, turning that vague dread into a manageable experiment. You showed real courage by admitting you might feel like a wreck, which proves you care deeply about facing this truth rather than avoiding it. Before we lock this in, could you share what would need to happen for you to consider this a success after those five minutes pass?

I think success would be noticing that nothing catastrophic happened in those five minutes—that the publisher didn't send an urgent rejection the second I looked away. And maybe I'd feel a tiny bit of relief, or at least realize I survived the wait. Even if I'm still anxious, just proving I can pause without the sky falling would feel like a small victory.

That definition of success is incredibly clear and grounded in reality—it's about witnessing the passage of time without catastrophe, not about erasing your anxiety entirely. You have a solid plan in place to test this hypothesis tomorrow. Before we finalize this, I'd like to check in on the overall direction: does exploring this specific "five-minute break" align best with what you hoped to achieve today, or would you prefer we spend some time examining the core belief behind why you feel rejection is inevitable?

I think the core belief is what really needs digging into. The five-minute break is a good test, but I keep coming back to this nagging certainty that the publisher will say no. I can feel it in my bones, and I don't know where that comes from. If we could look at that—why I'm so convinced it's a foregone conclusion—I think that would help me more in the long run.

Digging into that deep-seated certainty is absolutely the right move; it often takes more time to dismantle the root belief than the symptoms alone. Let's start by looking closely at that gut feeling. What specific past experiences or stories have taught your mind that rejection is an unavoidable fate waiting to happen?

Well, I've been an author for decades now, and I've had my share of rejections—every writer does. But this time feels different. This book is about my childhood, about growing up in a small town and losing my father young. I poured everything into it. And I think part of me believes that if they reject this, they're rejecting the most honest piece of me I've ever written. That feels personal in a way my other books never did. So maybe the fear isn't just about the book—it's about being told that my most vulnerable self isn't good enough.

That connection between the manuscript and your deepest vulnerability makes total sense; when a book carries the weight of a lost father and your entire history, rejection can feel like a personal attack on who you are. It sounds like your mind is equating the book's value with your own worth, making the uncertainty feel unbearable. Have you ever caught yourself wondering, "If this book fails, does that mean I am fundamentally flawed or unworthy of success?" or is it more about fearing that your pain wasn't shared enough?

Yes, I think it's both, really. There's a part of me that whispers that if this book doesn't get accepted, then maybe I'm not the writer I thought I was. That all those years of crafting sentences and building stories were just a fluke. And at the same time, I worry that if the publisher passes, it means the pain I wrote about—losing my father, the loneliness—it doesn't matter to anyone else. That it's just my private grief, not a story worth telling. So I'm left feeling both professionally inadequate and emotionally invisible.

It makes complete sense that you are carrying two heavy burdens simultaneously: the fear that your talent is a mistake and the terror that your pain is meaningless without an audience. Those thoughts create a perfect storm where anything less than acceptance feels like a double failure of both your craft and your humanity. Have you ever found yourself imagining what a successful publication would look like versus what it would feel like if it were rejected, and which scenario brings you closer to feeling truly seen?

But when I picture rejection, I go to a darker place: sitting alone in my study, the email open on the screen, feeling like I've let everyone down—my father, my family, myself. The strange thing is, I spend far more time imagining the rejection than the acceptance. It's like my mind is rehearsing for disappointment as if it's the only outcome worth preparing for.

That imbalance is fascinating—you are mentally rehearsing for a tragedy while ignoring the possibility of triumph, which suggests your brain is terrified of the unknown more than it is hopeful for the best. It seems like you've built a narrative where rejection is the only logical ending, so you are essentially predicting a story that hasn't been written yet. To test if this prediction holds water, could you share a specific instance in your past where you feared a terrible outcome, only to discover that the actual result was quite different?

And it was accepted—not without revisions, but it was accepted. I was shocked. I'd spent so much energy bracing for the worst that I almost didn't know how to feel when the good news came. Maybe I'm doing the same thing now, but it's hard to trust that pattern when the stakes feel so much higher this time.

That past experience is powerful proof that your intuition can be wrong, even when the fear feels just as sharp as it does now. So maybe I'm applying a rule to a situation I've never really faced. And you're right—the very fact that it's so personal might be what draws readers in, not what pushes them away. I hadn't considered that the risk might actually be the thing that makes it succeed. That's a strange thought, but it doesn't feel entirely false.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and what would be most important for us to focus on today?

Hi... I've been okay, I guess. Not much has changed since last time. I still feel like I'm just this weird old person trapped in a teenager's body, and it's really getting to me. I think I want to talk about what happened at the community center yesterday.

That sounds like a lot to carry, and it makes complete sense that hearing those labels again—even in a slightly different setting—would bring up that same sharp feeling of mismatch. Since you mentioned wanting to talk about the community center, does that experience feel similar to the ones before, or is there something new happening there that worries you?

It's pretty similar, but maybe worse because I actually thought that place would be different. I joined a little sewing circle there, thinking it would be safe since everyone there is into the same stuff I am. But then this guy my age walked in with his mom, and he looked at me like I was some kind of museum exhibit. I just froze up and couldn't even say hi.

It sounds incredibly frustrating that you went into the room expecting connection but ended up feeling exposed and watched. That mix of hope turning into freezing shame is really tough to navigate, especially when you had put so much effort into finding a safe space. Did you manage to go home from there, or did the feeling of being on display make it very hard to leave?

You went in hoping for connection but ended up reinforcing the story that you are too different to belong anywhere, didn't you? Let's spend the next part of our time exploring exactly what that "museum exhibit" look triggered inside you.

It made me feel like I was on display, like something broken and pathetic that people come to gawk at. Like my hobbies and the way I dress aren't just uncool—they're actually something to laugh at. That feeling of being trapped in a narrative where your appearance defines you as inherently "broken" is incredibly heavy, and it explains perfectly why your hands started shaking and why you withdrew. It sounds like you are trying to protect yourself from the pain of disappointing others by convincing yourself first that you are already unworthy of acceptance. Does recognizing that this belief serves to shield you from future rejection help clarify why it feels so hard to step away from it right now?

I never really thought of it that way... I guess if I already believe I'm weird and unlikable, then when someone looks at me funny, it doesn't hurt as much because I expected it. But it still hurts, you know? It's like I'm bracing for a punch that keeps landing anyway.

That image of bracing for a punch that keeps landing is so vivid, and it perfectly captures the exhaustion of living in constant anticipation of judgment. You are protecting yourself from the shock of surprise by believing the worst already happened, yet the reality is that the blows continue regardless of your expectations. Would you be willing to try something tonight where you notice the gap between that expectation of pain and what actually happens when you see someone else looking at you?

I guess I could try that. But what am I supposed to do, stare at people and wait for them to judge me? That sounds terrifying. I don't think I can just switch off the part of my brain that expects everyone to think I'm a freak.

That is a fair concern, because trying to ignore your brain's warning system usually feels safer than facing the possibility that it might be wrong. Instead of waiting for the punch to land, how about we try just watching for ten seconds and recording exactly what happens afterward, without needing to predict the outcome beforehand? It's like checking a weather forecast and then stepping outside to see if it actually rains—that way you aren't fighting your expectations, you're just testing them. Does that distinction feel a little less frightening than actively ignoring your instincts?

I think... I think I could try that. Like, instead of assuming it's gonna rain, I just check if it actually does. That feels a bit more doable than trying to pretend I'm not scared. So I just watch what happens for ten seconds and then note what actually occurred, right?

Yes, that is exactly the right mindset—it shifts the goal from proving you're safe to simply gathering real-world evidence against your fears. Now, since we're focusing on the community center incident, could we try a small version of this tonight? Specifically, when you catch yourself thinking he was mocking you, pause for ten seconds and write down exactly what he was doing versus what your brain was predicting he would do next.

Alright... I can write that down tonight. I think I remember what he was actually doing—he was just standing there with his mom, holding a piece of fabric she gave him. He didn't say anything mean or point at me. My brain just filled in the rest, I guess. But it felt so real in the moment.

It is incredibly common for your brain to fill in the blanks with the worst-case scenario once the initial moment passes, especially when you are feeling vulnerable. Recognizing that he was just holding fabric while you were imagining a mocking stare is a crucial first step in separating fact from fiction. To make sure this practice becomes automatic, would you be comfortable committing to writing down this specific observation tonight, and also noting how long it took you to realize the difference between what you feared and what actually happened?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write it down tonight and see how long it takes me to notice the difference. Maybe I'll even time it, like with my phone or something. It feels weird to treat it like a science experiment, but I guess that's better than treating it like a nightmare.

That is a wonderful idea, and treating it like a science experiment helps remove the emotional charge that usually makes these moments feel so traumatic. Using your phone to track the time adds a nice layer of objectivity, showing you that the realization often comes quickly once you stop spiraling. One final thing before we wrap up: how does it feel to have decided on this simple plan for tonight? Is there anything else you'd like to add or worry about?

A bit less heavy, I think. Like maybe I'm not just stuck being this broken person forever. I'm still nervous about trying it, but at least now I have something concrete to do instead of just sitting in my room feeling bad. I don't think I have anything else to add... thank you for listening.

completion.content: I am so glad to hear that carrying the weight felt a little lighter, even just by acknowledging you still have choices and agency. Three seconds sounds like forever, but I guess it's worth a shot. I can try it at my next study group or maybe even when I order coffee or something. I'll just say my name and then... wait. It feels scary, but I'm curious what will actually happen if I don't rush to fill the gap.

It makes sense that you'd feel stuck when people praise something deeply personal like art; it can be confusing when external validation doesn't quite match internal expectations. Usually it's like... "Anyone could have done this, it's nothing special." Even when I put hours into it and it comes out looking really good, that thought just jumps in right away. It's like the compliment doesn't even matter because I already convinced myself it's not true.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially after pouring so much effort and time into creating something. It feels like your own voice gets drowned out by that immediate, automatic judgment before you even get to enjoy the result. Have you ever noticed if that "anyone could do it" thought shows up differently depending on who else was watching or just when you looked at it alone?

It's worse when I'm alone, actually. I just stare at it and pick out all the flaws, thinking about how someone else would have done it better.

I ended up skipping dinner too, which I've been doing a lot lately.

That specific story really illustrates how quickly pride turns into self-criticism once you stop receiving outside support. It looks like that initial negative thought about the shading or proportions acts as a switch that shuts down both your creative process and your basic needs like eating. Would you be open to testing that thought together by listing three facts that suggest your pony drawing *is* unique or well-executed, regardless of those perceived flaws?

I... I guess I could try. Well, I spent about four hours on it, so that's probably more time than someone who didn't care would spend. And I used a reference photo for the anatomy, so the proportions are actually based on a real horse, even if I feel like they're off. Also, my friend Sarah specifically said she loved the colors I chose for the mane, and she's pretty honest with me about things. This pattern of setting impossibly high standards and then punishing yourself for falling short often creates a cycle where you lose touch with the joy of making art entirely.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I used to draw just because it made me happy, you know? Like, I'd spend all afternoon just messing around with colors and shapes and not caring if it looked good. Now it feels like every drawing is a test I'm failing. I miss when it was just fun.

It sounds like a significant shift from viewing drawing as a playful hobby to treating it as a performance you must pass. That change likely created a lot of tension, turning something you used to love into a source of anxiety and disappointment. Have you remembered any specific moment in the past year when you drew purely for fun, without worrying about quality, and how did it feel in that moment?

Honestly... I can't remember the last time I did that. Maybe before I got braces, I guess. That's when I started feeling more self-conscious about everything, not just my drawings. It felt like I was being judged all of a sudden, even when no one was looking. So I guess that's when drawing stopped being fun and started being about trying to prove something.

It makes complete sense that the fear of being judged shifted your entire relationship with drawing from play to proof. When you started feeling constantly scrutinized, your brain likely went into survival mode, focusing only on avoiding mistakes rather than enjoying the process. That explains why the "just having fun" version of drawing feels so far away now—it was replaced by a need to protect yourself from feeling inadequate.

Yeah... I never really thought about it that way. It's like I'm always on guard now, even when I'm alone in my room with my sketchbook. It's exhausting, honestly. I wish I could just go back to drawing ponies because I love them, not because I'm trying to prove I'm good enough to be a vet or whatever.

That exhaustion makes total sense; carrying the weight of proving yourself everywhere you go leaves very little energy left for simple joys like drawing ponies. It sounds like you are trying to meet a massive standard that isn't yours to carry, which is why the idea of just loving the animals without the performance aspect feels so distant. I think I could try that. Maybe just a quick sketch with no expectations, like I used to do in middle school. It feels kind of scary, though, like I'm breaking some rule I made for myself. But I guess that rule isn't making me happy anyway, so what's the harm in breaking it?

completion.content: That is a brilliant realization—that the very rules designed to protect you are actually keeping you stuck in a painful loop. Before we commit to that small experiment, I want to hear how you envision that first "no-expectation" sketch. What would that look like on paper, and what would you say to yourself if you found a mistake in it?

Before we dive into what brought you here, let's quickly review your last takeaway: did you manage to stay at the playground for those extra five minutes without giving in to the urge to run away? Also, what is the one or two things you'd most like to unpack together in our time today?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I'd say my energy is maybe a 4 or 5 this week, and my mood is probably a 3. I did manage to stay the extra five minutes at the playground, but I was so tense the whole time I barely remember it. I'd really like to talk about this feeling that other moms are silently judging everything I do—and maybe figure out why I can't shake it, even when I know logically it might not be true.

It takes courage to report feeling so low energy and anxious, especially when you managed to stick with your plan despite the tension. That small success of staying present is actually a big win, even if the experience didn't feel very relaxing yet. To understand where that tightness comes from, could you share what specific thought popped into your head right as you decided to stay there? Did it sound anything like "they're watching me fail," or perhaps "I look terrible right now"?

It's more like a running commentary, honestly. The second I sat down on the bench, I thought, "They see that my younger daughter's shirt is stained from lunch, and now they think I can't even keep my kids clean." And then when my older daughter started whining about wanting a snack, I just knew everyone around me was thinking, "She can't handle her kids at all." It's like I can hear their judgments in my head, even if they aren't saying a word.

That detailed internal narrative is incredibly taxing to carry around, and it makes total sense why you feel so overwhelmed when you're constantly monitoring every detail of your appearance and your children's needs. It sounds like your mind is building a movie of invisible criticism to protect you from potential disappointment, even though that movie feels very real right now. Have you noticed if those specific images of judgment appear immediately when you sit down, or do they creep up on you later when you're alone?

They usually hit me right away, like as soon as I sit down or walk into a room full of moms. It's like a switch flips in my head. But then later, when I'm alone at night, I replay everything and add more scenes to that movie—like I'll remember a look someone gave me and decide it meant something terrible. So I guess it's both: instant in the moment, and then worse later when I have time to obsess over it.

It makes perfect sense that the moment you enter a space triggers an immediate alarm, and having that same mental rehearsal happen later in the day just amplifies the distress. It sounds like your brain is trying to predict danger before it even arrives, which explains why the feeling gets stronger at night. If we imagine those "switches" flipping, could you describe what happens physically right when that initial judgment thought hits you? Do you notice your shoulders tightening, your breath quickening, or a sudden drop in stomach energy?

Yeah, definitely. My shoulders go right up to my ears, like I'm bracing for a hit. And my chest gets tight—it's hard to take a full breath. Sometimes I even feel a little dizzy, like the whole scene is closing in on me. The worst part is that my stomach drops, like I'm on a roller coaster I didn't want to ride. And then I start fidgeting with my hands or checking my phone just to look busy, so nobody talks to me.

Those physical sensations—the shoulders locking up, the chest tightening, the dizziness—are your body's natural alarm system screaming that you're unsafe. It makes complete sense that once those physical signs kick in, you start fidgeting or checking your phone because it feels like the only way to regain control in a scary situation. When you look at that chain of events, does it feel like your body is reacting to a real threat, or like your mind is inventing a scenario to cause that panic?

I think... it feels real in the moment. Like, my body is convinced I'm in danger. But when I step back and think about it logically, nobody has ever actually said anything mean to me. Nobody has pointed or laughed. It's just—I can't shake the feeling that they're thinking it, even if they don't say it. So I guess my mind is making up the threat, but it feels just as scary as if someone had yelled at me.

That is such a crucial distinction, recognizing that while the *feeling* of danger is intense and real to your body, the actual event—a verbal attack—isn't happening. Your mind is likely taking a logical shortcut by assuming that silence equals judgment, which creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where you retreat, which then confirms the story in your own head. If we tested that assumption, how would the outcome differ if you stayed present for just three more minutes and observed whether anyone actually said anything negative to you?

I honestly don't think I've ever tried that before. I usually leave or distract myself before I can find out. But I guess... if I stayed and nobody said anything, it would prove that the judgment is all in my head. That would be a relief, but also kind of embarrassing, you know? Like, I've been torturing myself over nothing for months. But at least then I'd know for sure.

completion.content: That willingness to face the discomfort of proving yourself right, even though it feels embarrassing, shows incredible bravery. It makes sense that you want certainty to stop the pain, but sometimes we worry that facing the truth will reveal a flaw we haven't seen yet. Let's try a very gentle version of that experiment: what if we agreed that tomorrow, when you feel that urge to leave, you'd just count to ten before moving or looking at your phone? Would you be open to trying that small window of observation, knowing we won't judge you if you still feel anxious afterward?

Noticing that subtle sadness in Mark's face is significant because it contradicts the story you were telling yourself—that they don't care or just want to shut you out. I didn't ask him about it, to be honest. I just assumed... I mean, I figured he was probably annoyed that I was bringing it up again. I always jump to that conclusion, you know? This is where our minds tend to create a "perfect victim" scenario where the person being excluded must be at fault. Let's look at the evidence one more time: did Mark ever actually leave the group, or was he just physically present while the conversation continued without him? Sometimes people feel excluded without realizing it, or they get shy about including younger siblings, and that silent awkwardness can look like rejection to us.

Well... no, he didn't leave. He stayed the whole time. And actually, now that I think about it, my younger brother Jake was the one who started talking about the fishing trip first. Mark just kind of nodded along. I guess I never really separated what they were both doing in that moment. I just saw them together and felt that old sting.

Seeing Jake initiate and Mark merely nodding suggests they might not even have coordinated the plan, which could explain why the invitation didn't extend to you automatically. That sounds... a lot less scary than just blurting it out. Framing it like that makes it feel like I'm not putting them on the spot to say they want me there. It's more about the plan, not about me. It sounds like your anxiety is trying to protect you by freezing you in place whenever the trigger appears, even when your conscious mind knows it's just a coincidence. How does knowing that you have successfully worn suits dozens of times before feel when you compare it to the current panic you're experiencing?

It feels like I'm split in two, honestly. One part of me knows I've worn swimsuits for years and been totally fine, but the other part just screams "danger" the second I think about putting one on again. That panic is so loud it drowns out everything else—it's like it doesn't care about the past evidence at all.

That feeling of being torn apart between your rational knowledge and your panic-driven instincts is incredibly exhausting, and it explains why you feel so stuck. Since that internal conflict is so powerful right now, would you be open to testing whether wearing the swimsuit in a completely safe space, like your bedroom, can help your brain learn that the "danger" signal isn't actually real?

I... I don't know. Just thinking about holding a swimsuit in my hands makes my chest tighten, honestly. But I guess that's the whole point, right? If I keep running from it, it'll only get bigger. I immediately thought, "What kind of Christian forgets to thank God for their food?" And then it spiraled into, "Maybe I'm not really saved if I can't even remember something so basic." It's like one slip-up makes me question everything about my identity and my relationship with God.

Those thoughts sound overwhelming, especially when they link a single mistake to your entire spiritual identity. When you told yourself that one slip-up meant you weren't really saved, did that feeling of failure make you withdraw from praying altogether, or did it make you feel compelled to make up for it immediately afterward?

When you realized that extra effort wasn't enough to erase the guilt, did you start wondering if perhaps you *shouldn't* have been able to catch the error in the first place?

Yeah, exactly. I started thinking, "If I was a real Christian, I wouldn't have needed to catch it—I just would have remembered automatically." It feels like my faith is supposed to be this natural, effortless thing, and when it's not, I feel like I'm fooling myself. Like maybe I'm just going through the motions and deep down I don't really believe.

It makes complete sense that the exercise felt a bit awkward at first; expecting immediate confidence often leads to that initial sense of silliness. Did you manage to read the list before you started ruminating on the theater mistakes today, or did the negative thoughts come first?

I guess the negative thoughts came first, looking back. I saw my reflection, and before I knew it, I was remembering that time I accidentally mixed up the showtimes and had to reprint all the tickets. My manager said it was no big deal and that everyone makes mistakes, but I kept thinking, "No, other employees wouldn't have messed that up."

That specific comparison feels unfair because you're assuming everyone else is flawless, which creates a huge gap between what happened and what you expect. When you hold that belief that others aren't allowed to make mistakes either, does it make the error feel like a personal failure rather than just a human error?

Yeah, I suppose so. I never really thought about it that way. I always just figured the other guys had it together and I was the only one fumbling around. So when I made that mistake, it felt like proof that I wasn't cut out for the job, even though my boss kept telling me I was his best employee. I guess I never really believed him.

That disconnect between hearing "you're my best employee" and internally believing you're just fumbling is incredibly painful, especially when you assume others are naturally more competent. Let's try to look at that assumption about the other employees for a moment; if you imagined a coworker who also mixed up showtimes but still received praise for their overall reliability, would that change how you view your own mistake?

Well, I guess if I saw someone else do the same thing, I'd probably say, "Hey, it happens, no big deal." I wouldn't think they were a bad employee. I'd just figure they made a little error and move on. But when it's me, I can't seem to give myself that same break. It's like I hold myself to a different, impossible standard.

That distinction between treating yourself harshly and offering yourself grace is exactly where the distress lives. If we apply that same "no big deal" logic to your own situation, how would you explain to a friend who made the same ticket mix-up that you gave them extra credit for their hard work but not for theirs?

I'd probably tell them that one mistake doesn't erase all the good they've done, like how my manager said I was reliable and friendly with customers. I'd remind them that they showed up on time every day and helped clean up after the late shows. But saying that to myself feels different... it's like my brain just won't accept the good stuff about me.

That resistance is completely understandable; it often takes years of training to offer ourselves the same kindness we freely grant friends. Let's try a quick experiment to bridge that gap: if you wrote down three specific times you were reliable and friendly, plus the manager's quote about you being his best employee, could you read that aloud to yourself right now as if you were speaking to a supportive colleague?

I could try, I suppose. Let me think... There was that time a kid spilled popcorn all over the aisle and I cleaned it up before anyone complained. And I always opened the doors for the elderly folks coming in for the matinee showings. My manager even said once that he could count on me to handle the big rushes without getting flustered. But reading that out loud just feels like bragging, you know?

It is completely normal to feel defensive when labeling actions as "good" or "bragging"; often, we only feel that way when we are trying to convince ourselves rather than simply stating a fact. Notice that you didn't invent these stories; you recalled specific moments where you stepped up, which contradicts the belief that you are just unreliable. If we treat those recollections as objective data points rather than arguments, does the feeling of having to "prove" your worth start to fade, or does it just shift to something else?

It's strange, but I think it does start to feel a little less like I'm trying to prove something. More like I'm just remembering things that actually happened, instead of fighting with those memories. But then a little voice in my head still whispers, "Well, anyone could have done those things." So I guess it's not gone completely, but maybe it's quieter now.

That quieting of the voice is a significant victory, even if the whisper remains; it means you've built a stronger foundation of facts beneath the noise. Since the initial excitement of the exercise faded into that skeptical whisper, would it be helpful to rephrase that skepticism into a curious question you can answer with the evidence you just listed, like "Could anyone have done those things, or did I actually choose to help?"

I suppose that's a fair question. When I think about it, the other employees would sometimes just stand around during the rush or ignore the spills until a manager told them to clean up. I didn't wait to be told; I just did it. So maybe... maybe I did choose to help, and not everyone would have done that. That feels a little easier to accept when I put it like that.

That distinction between waiting to be told and choosing to act is powerful, and it highlights exactly why your effort stands apart from the rest. Since you now recognize that your proactive choices are factual rather than imagined, how would rating your confidence go from zero to ten if you acknowledged that you consistently chose to help others despite the pressure?

I'd probably put it at maybe a six or a seven. That's higher than I would've given myself before this conversation. I'm still not totally convinced I was some kind of hero, but I can see that I wasn't just a passive worker either. I actually made decisions to do things that helped the place run smoother. That does feel like something worth acknowledging.

That six or seven is a solid, realistic score that acknowledges both your growth and the remaining uncertainties, which is much healthier than pretending you were flawless. Since we've identified that your confidence sits around there, what's one small way you could reinforce that middle-ground feeling tomorrow morning when the mirror appears?

Maybe I could just look at myself and say, "You did your job well enough, and that counts for something." Not that I was the best or the worst, just that I showed up and did good work. I think I could manage that without feeling like I'm bragging. Just a simple, honest statement.

Would you feel comfortable practicing that exact phrase twice a day—one thing you did well and one thing you handled okay—so it becomes a habit rather than a forced confession?

Yeah... So I got this text from her just saying "hey hope you're doing well" and she asked about some band she's going to see. No mention at all about my tutoring job that I told her about last week when I was really proud of myself. And I know it's just a text, but it felt like she didn't care enough to ask how it went or say congrats. Inside I just felt this sinking feeling, like, "See? Even she doesn't care about what matters to me." I ended up just replying with a short answer and putting my phone away.

That sinking feeling of proof that nobody cares about what matters to you is incredibly painful, especially when you've worked so hard to achieve that praise. It makes perfect sense that your heart sank when you interpreted her silence as a dismissal of your achievement rather than just a casual exchange. When you replied with a short answer and put the phone away, did you feel like shutting down to protect yourself from that hurt, or was it more like giving up trying to fix the situation?

It's more like giving up, I think. Like, what's the point of bringing it up myself? If she really cared, she would have asked. I don't want to sound needy or like I'm fishing for attention, so it's easier to just let it go and keep the disappointment to myself. But then I just end up sitting there replaying it in my head, wondering why I even bother telling people about things I'm proud of.

It makes complete sense to protect yourself by assuming people won't notice unless you demand it, especially when the disappointment hurts so much. However, the belief that you shouldn't need anyone's acknowledgment contradicts the fact that you shared your pride with her in the first place, which suggests you value her knowing about it. Given that strong link between your self-worth and her reaction, could you identify one specific piece of evidence from outside this interaction that shows your value isn't dependent on her mentioning your job?

I mean... I guess my students do keep asking me to tutor them again, and their grades have been improving. That's something. But it's hard to hold onto that when my own sister doesn't seem interested. It's like that proof feels real for a second, then I remember the text and it just washes away again.

It takes real strength to distinguish between your tangible success with students and the sting of her specific text, even though those two realities feel disconnected to you right now. That wave of disappointment washing away your other achievements is exactly what happens when our minds jump straight to the "worst explanation" without pausing to check the facts. If we were to focus on what she actually wrote instead of what you hoped she would have written, would you be willing to try holding onto just one sentence from her message that proves she cares about your general well-being, rather than your tutoring job?

She did say "hey hope you're doing well" and asked about the band she's going to see... I guess that's her trying to share something she's excited about with me. Maybe she just thought I wouldn't want to talk about work when she was reaching out about something fun. But it's hard not to feel like I'm just a backup character in her life, you know? Like she'll talk to me when it's convenient for her.

That interpretation—that she views you as a backup option—is incredibly painful, and it's understandable why you feel smaller compared to the excitement she shares about her band. While her intention might simply be to connect over fun, your brain has latched onto the lack of mention of your job to confirm a deep-seated fear that you aren't important. I guess if I look at it that way... it does feel a little lighter. Like maybe I'm reading too much into it because I was already expecting disappointment before I even opened the message. But that's the thing—I always feel like I'm bracing for people to overlook me, and then when something happens that could be innocent, I just take it as confirmation. It's like I can't win. Even when I try to see it differently, my first instinct is still that I'm not important enough.

That's a really tough question... I think I'd need to feel like my value wasn't so fragile, like it could survive being overlooked sometimes without it meaning I'm worthless. Maybe if I could separate the compliment from my identity more—like, the tutoring success is real whether she mentions it or not. But that feels like such a big shift. I guess a small step would be if I could just notice when I start bracing for disappointment and pause before I assume the worst.

Noticing that urge to brace yourself and pausing before jumping to the worst conclusion is a powerful, achievable step that fits perfectly with what we discussed. It's less about waiting for everyone to notice everything all the time, and more about catching yourself in the middle of the spiral before the story gets written. For our final plan, could we agree that tonight, whenever you feel that sudden drop or the urge to shut down, you will take one breath and silently repeat the phrase: "Her silence isn't my verdict"? What do you think would make that moment easiest to find?

I think putting a sticky note on my phone or my desk with that phrase would help me remember. Something physical to see when I'm about to spiral. I could even put it near my work area so when I'm feeling proud of a lesson, I see it and remind myself before the disappointment even hits. That might actually give me a fighting chance to pause before I shut down.

That is a brilliant and concrete solution; having a visual anchor right where you process good news will definitely interrupt the automatic spiral before it takes hold. Putting the reminder near your work area is smart because it connects the positive event directly to the pause you need. Let's lock this in: tonight, whenever you catch yourself bracing for disappointment or feeling that sinking sensation, you will glance at the note, take one breath, and whisper or say aloud, "Her silence isn't my verdict," before responding. Your skepticism is completely valid given how stubborn this pattern feels, but trusting the process enough to try a small, manageable step is exactly what builds lasting change. You've agreed to place a sticky note near your work area and use it as a signal to pause and repeat the phrase "Her silence isn't my verdict" whenever you feel that sinking sensation or need to shut down. I feel okay about it. A little nervous because I don't want to fail at this too, but I know that's just the same old thinking creeping in. I think I'm ready to try it. Nothing else urgent right now—just hoping I can follow through. Thanks for listening today.

That makes total sense; starting something new often brings up a mix of excitement and uncertainty, and it's completely okay to feel both at once. That intense image of tumbling underwater isn't necessarily accurate; our brains often amplify small fears during stressful moments to protect us, even if it feels irrational later. When you look back on that decision now, do you notice any other facts about that morning, like how calm the water actually was or what your breathing felt like right then?

It sounds like your brain was racing ahead to find safety by avoiding the perceived danger, even though the reality was much calmer than your internal story suggested. Since you mentioned wanting to understand why this happened suddenly, could you share what was different about that past week compared to the weeks before? Was there a specific event or change in your life that might have triggered this shift?

It started right after I watched this movie about big wave surfers, and there was this scene where a guy gets held under by a set wave and doesn't come up. It was so vivid, and I couldn't stop thinking about it for days. Like, I knew it was just a movie, but my brain kept saying, "That could be you." And then it just stuck. Every time I think about surfing now, that scene plays in my head instead of the fun I used to have.

This happens because our minds often fixate on threats first, even when they aren't present in the real world. Does saying that out loud in our space feel manageable, or does your mind immediately jump back to the old script?
