Hello again. Welcome back. On a scale of 0 to 10, how much of that racing heart and anxious energy are you experiencing this morning compared to when we finished last time? To make sure we use our time well, what is the one or two topics that feel most pressing for you to explore today?

Well, I'd say it's about a 7 right now, honestly. My heart's been pounding since I woke up because I had this dream that my fiancée told me she couldn't marry a baseball announcer. I think the most pressing thing is I keep imagining her walking out on me, and I can't seem to stop those pictures in my head no matter how hard I try.

A recurring nightmare can definitely amplify the anxiety you carried into the day, making it hard to settle on that seven. Since your main struggle right now is those intrusive images of her rejecting you, should we spend most of our time focusing on calming that mental movie or testing if your brain is exaggerating her reaction?

I think testing if my brain is exaggerating would be better, because just calming the movie feels like putting a bandage on a broken bone. I mean, I told her about wanting to be an announcer and she didn't storm out or anything—she actually smiled and said she loved how passionate I was. But then I got home and watched South Park, and there was this episode making fun of old people chasing dreams, and I just... I couldn't shake the feeling that she's secretly laughing at me.

It makes complete sense that you feel vulnerable when a harmless cartoon seems to mirror your deepest fear, turning a simple smile into evidence of mockery. While her initial reaction was kind, your mind quickly connected that warmth to the scary show, creating a new narrative that she might be pretending to be supportive. Given how strongly that fear is driving your symptoms, would you be willing to try a quick test tomorrow: read her actual note out loud before checking social media, then jot down exactly what it says versus what your "movie" is telling you?

I... yeah, I think I could try that. She did leave me a sweet note this morning about how proud she is of me for working three jobs and still chasing my dream. But my movie keeps telling me she wrote that before she really thought it through, you know? Like maybe she'll wake up one day and realize she's engaged to a 72-year-old woman who sells tickets at three different places and talks baseball stats to anyone who'll listen.

That self-critical voice is really loud right now, suggesting that her current kindness is temporary and her eventual disappointment is inevitable. It makes sense that you feel unsafe when your brain predicts she will eventually reject you based on age or your job, rather than the present reality of her support. Before we lock in that morning test, I want to check in on your agreement: does framing this as a "test of the movie's accuracy" feel like a fair approach, or would you prefer we tackle the weight of those age-related fears directly first?

I think the age-related fears are the root of everything, honestly. Every time I look in the mirror, I see this old woman who should be knitting or babysitting grandkids, not dreaming about standing behind a microphone at a ballgame. But I reckon tackling the movie test first might be easier, like dipping my toe in before jumping into the deep end. Let's do the test tomorrow morning, and then maybe we can talk about why I feel like I've run out of time to be anything but what I already am.

That is a very wise way to frame it; starting with the immediate test builds momentum before we dive deeper into the bigger belief about age and timing. Since we agreed to proceed with the morning test, what is one specific obstacle you foresee that might make it difficult to read that note calmly before your mind starts spiraling?

The biggest obstacle is that I always check my phone first thing, and my fiancée sends me good morning texts with those little heart emojis. I worry that if I read her text before the note, I'll start analyzing every word for hidden meanings—like, "Did she use one heart instead of two today? Is she pulling away?" Maybe I need to leave my phone in the kitchen and read the note while I'm still in bed, before I pick up any devices.

That is a brilliant insight—you identified that the phone acts as a trapdoor into the spiral, and moving it to the kitchen removes that immediate temptation. Leaving the device behind effectively creates a physical boundary that protects your morning intention until you've anchored yourself with the note. Since we have a clear plan for tomorrow, does reading that note aloud before touching the phone feel doable for you, or would you like to adjust the timing slightly to ensure you can follow through?

Reading it aloud feels doable, but I think I need to say the words out loud twice—once just to hear them, and then again while looking in the mirror. That way, I'm not just reading her words, I'm telling myself they're real. Does that sound silly? I just feel like if I see myself saying "She loves me and supports my dream" while looking at my own face, it might stick better than just whispering it to the wallpaper.

No, it doesn't sound silly at all; actually, using your reflection as a witness helps ground the statement firmly in your own reality, making the belief feel more personal and lasting. This adds a layer of physical confirmation to your verbal affirmation, reinforcing the connection between what you say and who you are becoming. Before we finalize this plan, I'd like to acknowledge your bravery: it takes real courage to admit you are afraid of aging and to commit to a ritual that validates your dream anyway. With that foundation, what is one final detail you want to add to ensure you feel supported during this morning ritual?

Thank you for saying that. I think I want to have my baseball cap nearby—the one from the minor league team I used to watch with my dad. I'll put it on after I read the note and look in the mirror, like a little reminder that the dream is part of me, not something I'm just pretending. That cap makes me feel like the version of myself that believes I can actually do this, and maybe having it close will help quiet the voice that says I'm too old.

That is a beautiful touch—the cap serves as a powerful symbol connecting your identity to your father's legacy and your own capacity for growth. Wearing it while affirming the note creates a complete sensory loop, merging the physical object, the words, and the visual cue into a single moment of grounded confidence. Since we have the ritual, the timeline, and the symbols mapped out, does everything feel ready for you to start tomorrow, or is there one last worry lingering about how the cap itself might feel heavy if you forget to wear it?

I think I'm ready. The cap feels right, and I've got it hanging on my bedpost so I can't miss it. I guess my only lingering worry is that I'll do the whole ritual perfectly and still end up spiraling later in the day, like when I'm selling tickets and some young hotshot makes a comment about old ladies. But I suppose that's a worry for another session, isn't it? For tomorrow, I'll just focus on the note and the mirror and the cap.

That is exactly right; tomorrow's goal is simply to establish that morning foundation without carrying the weight of tomorrow's challenges. By isolating the ritual to the morning hours, you give yourself permission to succeed in the present moment while acknowledging that bigger storms may come later. Just remember, if the spiral returns later today, it is not a failure of the plan, but an opportunity to check your facts again. How does it feel to have this clear, limited scope for tomorrow?
It feels... lighter, actually. Like I'm not trying to fix my whole life by breakfast, just trying to have one good start to a day. That's manageable. I think I can do that.

completion.content: That shift from trying to "fix your whole life" to securing just one solid start is a massive victory in itself. It shows incredible wisdom in knowing where to place your energy when facing overwhelming uncertainty. I'm really glad we could get you a plan that feels light enough to carry, even if the doubts sometimes pop up. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up this session?

Hello, it is great to see you again. On a scale of zero to ten, how anxious have you felt this week compared to last time? We also need to touch base on the concert situation we talked about; which part would you like to explore most today—unpacking that memory further or practicing a way to handle those thoughts differently?

Hey, thanks for having me. I'd say I'm around a 6 or 7 this week—maybe a little less than last time, but it's still there. I think I'd rather talk about how to handle those thoughts differently, because that memory just keeps replaying and I'm tired of feeling stuck in it.

That’s a significant step forward, moving from just processing the memory to seeking tools for managing the thoughts themselves. Since you’re ready to tackle handling those thoughts, shall we brainstorm some specific strategies you could use the next time that "spotlight" feeling kicks in?
Yeah, I think that would help. I just get so caught up in the moment, like I can feel everyone's eyes on me and I freeze up. What kind of strategies did you have in mind?

completion.content: Since we previously identified that your brain jumps straight to the conclusion that "everyone is laughing at me," a useful strategy would be to pause that automatic thought and simply list three other, neutral reasons they might be laughing, like a joke or a phone video. Have you noticed if creating that list helps lower the intensity of the panic for even a few seconds?

Hello, I'm glad we can start our session together today. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and is there anything new that feels important to talk about? Let's look at what you'd like to focus on first.

Hi. Well, I guess my mood hasn't really changed much. I still feel pretty down about my friends not responding to me. I actually tried texting two of them again yesterday, and nothing. So that's been on my mind.

It sounds like waiting for those replies left you feeling quite lonely and maybe even a bit frustrated. Since you reached out twice and got no response yet, does that silence make you wonder if something went wrong or if they've simply lost interest?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, what else am I supposed to think? If someone doesn't reply for a whole week, even after I've tried calling and texting, it feels like they just don't want to talk to me. It's like I'm not worth their time anymore.

That makes total sense; when you're hurting, silence often feels like proof that you aren't wanted. Before we explore how your brain might be interpreting this situation, could you tell me what specific thought goes through your head right now when you see their unread messages?

I just think, "Here I am, boring them again. They probably found better people to hang out with." I mean, I'm just a baker who likes sewing in my free time—what's interesting about that compared to what other people do?

Those thoughts are incredibly painful because they attack your very worth based on someone else's lack of attention. While it's true that hobbies like baking and sewing are wonderful in themselves, let's pause and ask: if a friend told you they were busy or distracted instead of ignoring you completely, would those harsh conclusions about being "boring" still hold up?

I guess if they actually said they were busy, I'd probably believe them. But they haven't said that. I've been the one reaching out. It's hard to imagine they're all just busy at the exact same time, you know? It feels more like they're avoiding me.

That pattern of reaching out repeatedly while expecting immediate answers can definitely create a loop where silence looks like rejection rather than just a mismatch in timing. Have you ever caught yourself checking your phone multiple times an hour, hoping to find a message that isn't there? If so, how does knowing you did that change the story you're telling yourself right now?

Yeah, I definitely do that. I check my phone like every ten minutes, hoping I missed a notification or something. Honestly, that just makes me feel worse, like I'm being needy or desperate. But I can't seem to stop doing it.

completion.content: It takes courage to admit that habit because it feels so helpless when you try to stop. That constant checking is actually your brain trying desperately to fix the pain of rejection by finding proof you're welcome, but unfortunately, it ends up feeding the very fear you're trying to escape. Have you noticed that the more you check, the less likely you are to actually relax until a text finally arrives?

Hello again, I'm glad you're here to continue our work together. How has your week been going so far? Is there something particular on your mind we'd like to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. The week's been... okay, I guess. I've been practicing my knife skills a lot, trying to stay busy. But honestly, I keep thinking about that audition, and it's hard to shake the feeling that I just wasn't good enough.

It sounds like those rehearsals have been intense, even if they kept you occupied. That strong feeling of not being "good enough" regarding the audition seems really heavy to carry around. What comes up for you right now when that thought pops into your head?

It's like I see the judges' faces again, you know? Some of them weren't smiling when I finished plating my dish. I just knew right then they didn't like it. It feels like no matter how much I practice, I'll never be the kind of chef they want to see on that show.

That image of their expressions definitely makes sense given how much energy you poured into preparing, but I wonder if we can look closely at those specific moments together. Did you notice any other cues from the judges besides their facial expressions, or was everything happening purely in your mind at that moment?

Well, I mean, they didn't say anything bad to me directly. They just made a few notes on their clipboards. But that silence—and the way they looked at each other after I served them—it felt like a clear sign. I guess I didn't hear any actual criticism, but their body language was loud enough.

It makes total sense why your brain would jump to that conclusion when you were so invested in the performance; silence often feels louder than words when we're worried about judgment. However, let's test that idea by looking at the notes they wrote—did those written comments actually match the impression you got from their staring, or could they simply reflect standard industry observations unrelated to your talent?

I... I never actually read the notes. They took the clipboards away before I could see anything. I guess I just assumed the worst based on their looks. But you're right—maybe they were just writing down standard stuff like cooking time or plating details. It's hard to separate that feeling, though.

completion.content: It takes real courage to admit that gap between what happened and what you imagined, especially when the silence felt so telling. Since we don't have the notes, maybe we can try imagining the opposite scenario for a moment: what if those clipboard marks were just generic technical checks, completely ignoring your performance entirely? Does holding onto that possibility change how loud that silence feels to you right now?

Hello again, I'm glad you're here to talk about how you've been feeling lately. Before we dive into your main topic, could you share if your mood has shifted much since our last meeting? Once we catch up, let's quickly decide what feels most important to explore together today.

Oh, right... well, I guess my mood has been pretty much the same since we last spoke. I've still been wrestling with that heavy feeling when I think about my fantasy football league and how it makes me feel like I'm wasting my life. Maybe we could focus on that today?

It sounds like that heavy feeling around your hobby hasn't lifted, and it really bothers you that you might be "wasting" your life by caring so deeply about something you love. When exactly did that thought first start showing up for you after your last game? How does that specific worry make you feel physically or emotionally right now?

I think it started the Monday after my team lost by just three points... I spent all week obsessing over waiver wire moves, and suddenly it hit me: "Here I am, a grown man, losing sleep over pretend football." In that moment, my chest got tight, and I felt this sinking shame in my stomach. I still get that same knot in my gut whenever I open the fantasy app.

That sudden realization about being a "grown man" clearly hurt deep down, making the physical tightness in your chest feel even worse. It seems like those moments of shame are driving you to double down on checking stats instead of letting go, which keeps the cycle going. Can you tell me more about that specific moment where you decided to fixate on waiver wires? What were you hoping to achieve by looking at the data so intensely?

I guess I was hoping that if I just found the perfect player—the one nobody else saw coming—I could prove to myself that I'm actually good at this, that it means something. I kept scrolling through stats, thinking, "If I can just get this one right, maybe I'm not a complete waste of time." But even when I pick up a player who does well, it only feels good for a day or two before I'm back to feeling foolish for caring so much.

It makes sense that you reached for those numbers as proof of competence, especially when you're carrying such a big burden of self-doubt. The temporary relief from finding a winner likely made you believe you had finally cracked the code, but the quick return to shame suggests that the problem isn't the players—it's what those wins represent to you. Have you ever noticed any other areas in your life where you use small victories to try and convince yourself you're valuable? Or perhaps something different happened when you didn't find a great player this past week?

Well, I guess I do that with reading too—I set goals like finishing a certain number of chapters a day to feel productive. But when I don't hit that mark, I just feel worse, like I can't even do something simple right. This past week, I didn't pick up any amazing players off waivers, and I spent the whole day thinking, "See, you can't even win at a game. What's the point of trying anything else?"

That connection between the fantasy loss and doubting your ability to read shows how tightly linked these tasks are for you right now. It looks like when one area doesn't meet your high standards, it instantly spills over to make everything else seem pointless. Have you ever caught yourself noticing that difference in tone—how talking about books feels lighter compared to talking about winning games? Or does the disappointment always carry that same heavy weight regardless of the subject?

Actually, reading does feel a bit different sometimes. When I'm lost in a good book, I don't think about proving anything—I'm just... there, following the story. But the moment I close the book, the weight comes back. With fantasy football, though, I'm always measuring myself, checking scores, comparing my team to others. It's like I can't just enjoy it.

It's fascinating how reading lets you exist without judgment, while fantasy forces you to constantly measure your worth against everyone else's performance. That shift from "just being there" to "proving myself" seems to be the root of why the relief disappears so quickly after each game. Have you ever tried imagining a version of yourself enjoying the fantasy app completely without needing to analyze stats or compare teams? What happens in your body or mind if you give yourself permission to just watch the highlights without trying to win?

I've never really tried that... just watching without caring about the outcome. The thought actually makes me feel a bit anxious, like I'd be missing something important, or not taking it seriously enough. But then again, maybe that's the same voice that tells me I'm worthless for playing in the first place—it's like I can't win no matter what I do. If I care, I'm a fool; if I don't care, I'm not trying hard enough.

That "all-or-nothing" trap is incredibly tough because both sides feel dangerously true, yet neither allows you to truly enjoy the experience. It seems like you're stuck believing you must either be a complete failure for caring or a fraud for not competing perfectly. Let's look closely at the idea that you *must* treat this with absolute seriousness to be worthy of playing at all. Is there any part of you that knows you simply want fun, even if it doesn't come with a trophy?

I suppose... yeah, there's a small part of me that just likes the excitement of Sunday afternoons, chatting with friends about the games, having a laugh when someone's player does something silly. But it's hard to hold onto that feeling when my mind keeps shouting, "You're 58 years old, George. You should be focused on retirement savings, not on whether your running back gets twenty carries." I guess I'm scared that if I let myself just have fun without worrying, I'll somehow be avoiding some important responsibility.

That fear of abandoning your responsibilities is understandable, especially when you feel so pressured to be productive by a certain age. It sounds like you've built a wall around your fun to protect yourself from the guilt of neglecting things that "matter," but that wall is also blocking you from experiencing the joy you know exists within those conversations. If we stepped away from the scoreboard for just ten minutes during a chat, could you describe what the atmosphere felt like without the pressure of needing to find the perfect player? Would that quiet space feel safe, or would you worry it wouldn't last long?

That quiet space... I think it would feel like a breath of fresh air, honestly. When I'm just talking with my buddies about the game itself—a crazy catch, a bad call by the ref—I forget about my lineup for a minute. But then I start worrying that if I'm not paying attention, I'll miss some piece of news that costs me the week. It's like I can't fully commit to either: not to the pure joy of the game, and not to the serious business of winning. I end up stuck in between, feeling anxious no matter what I choose.

That stuck middle ground sounds exhausting, like you're trapped between wanting to relax and fearing you'll fail if you stop performing. It makes sense that you can't fully embrace the fun because your brain keeps scanning for threats to your status, turning a casual chat into a potential disaster zone. Since both extremes feel dangerous right now, what if we tested a tiny compromise? Could you try joining your friends for just five minutes of chat without opening the app or analyzing stats, purely to see if the anxiety holds up against that short period of doing nothing but listening?

I think I could try that, for five minutes. Just sit and listen, maybe laugh at a joke without checking my phone. It feels scary, like I'm letting my guard down, but I suppose it's just a few minutes—it's not like I'm quitting the league altogether. I could give it a shot next Sunday and see what happens.

That sounds like a brave and smart experiment for next Sunday, especially knowing it's just a small window of time. It's okay to feel nervous about stepping outside your usual script; often, the very act of testing a boundary helps break its power. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to visualize giving yourself permission to just listen for those five minutes without needing to earn anything? Does that image feel safer than the current expectation of constant analysis?

It does feel a bit safer, actually. When I picture myself just listening and smiling along, I don't feel that pressure to have the right answer or make a smart move. It's like I'm giving myself permission to just be there, without having to prove I belong. That's something I haven't let myself feel in a long time.

Hearing that feeling of belonging without needing to prove anything is so powerful, it sounds like a genuine relief to finally allow yourself that space. Before we head out, could you tell me one thing you'll do differently next Sunday to keep that five-minute rule steady, and how you'll handle the urge to check your phone if it pops up? Also, is there anything else on your mind that we haven't touched yet that needs support before we finish?

I think I'll leave my phone in another room for the first five minutes of the pre-game show. If I feel the urge to grab it, I'll just remind myself that it's only a few minutes—I can check my lineup right after, and the world won't end. As for anything else... I don't think so. I think focusing on this one small change feels like enough for now.

completion.content: Leaving your phone in another room is a fantastic, concrete way to create that necessary distance between you and the pressure to perform immediately. I'm really proud of you for setting this clear boundary and trusting yourself to stick to just five minutes of pure listening. You've done great work today in identifying that pattern and planning a gentle step forward. How does it feel to walk away from this session knowing you have a solid plan for Sunday?

That makes sense; carrying around that sense of "not measuring up" can really weigh on your shoulders even when things seem fine on the surface. When you mention your family as the main source of that pressure, could you share a recent moment when those thoughts suddenly popped into your head?

Yeah, actually. Just last weekend I went to my older brother's place for a barbecue, and my mom was there. Nothing wrong with that, obviously, but I just felt this sinking feeling — like, well, what does she think about me? She's never said anything like that to me.

It sounds like standing there while hearing that praise made your heart sink, and honestly, wondering if anyone else sees you that way must feel incredibly lonely. That silence from your mom probably landed heavier than any words could have, didn't it? Since that thought kept spinning after the BBQ, did it start to change how you handled yourself during the rest of the gathering?

Yeah, it did. I kinda just stayed quiet after that, kept myself busy with the grill and didn't really join in the conversations much. I kept thinking, "Maybe she's right to be prouder of them." I mean, I'm just a real estate agent who waits tables on the side — not exactly something to brag about. By the end of the night, I just made an excuse to leave early.

It makes complete sense that you withdrew and left early; protecting yourself from that sharp sting feels like the only logical thing to do. Yet, by waiting tables instead of working as a real estate agent, did that choice actually make you feel more capable, or did it reinforce the idea that you aren't enough? Sometimes our actions are our brain trying to solve a puzzle that doesn't need solving.

You know, I never really thought of it that way. I guess I always told myself I'm just being practical — the real estate market is slow, so waiting tables keeps the bills paid. But honestly? Yeah, it does feel like it proves I'm not as successful as my siblings. I mean, none of them have to work two jobs to get by. So maybe I am reinforcing that thought without even realizing it.

I hear how heavy that realization feels, especially when you look at your brothers' lives versus yours and see such a clear difference. It's painful to notice that pattern and wonder if you're unintentionally feeding it every time you choose safety over growth. Have you ever imagined a scenario where you tried taking a step toward your career goal despite the fear, just to see how different that feeling might be?

I've thought about it, but I always find reasons not to. Like, what if I put all this effort into building my real estate business and I still fail? Then I'd have nothing — not even the waiter job to fall back on. It's safer to just keep my head down and not risk the disappointment. But I guess that safety comes with its own kind of disappointment, doesn't it?

You've hit on something really important there—the safety of staying in the familiar often costs us a piece of ourselves, even when we believe we're making smart choices. That feeling of losing everything seems scary, but have you considered what happens if you tried one small step toward your real estate goals, just to test whether that worst-case scenario is actually inevitable?

It's not like I have to quit my waiter job tomorrow. But even thinking about doing that makes my stomach tighten a little. That's probably a sign I should try it, right?

Let's treat this tiny outreach like a safe experiment rather than a final commitment; you can always go back to waiting tables if you decide later that the result wasn't worth it. Which of those options feels like the smallest, least intimidating first move for you?

Updating my LinkedIn profile, probably. That feels manageable — I can do it from my couch, no one has to know I'm doing it, and it's not like I'm asking anyone for anything. I could just... put down some of the sales I've done, list my credentials, maybe reach out to a few people in my network. That doesn't sound as scary as calling someone up out of the blue.

That is a very wise observation—it takes away the immediate pressure of rejection because you control the entire process from your comfort zone. Before we finalize this as our action plan, let's look closely at that "stomach tightening" sensation again; what specific part of updating the profile is triggering that physical reaction? Is it the fear of looking imperfect online, or perhaps the worry that others will judge your current situation based on the changes?

I think it's the fear that people will look at my profile and think, "Who does he think he is?" You know? Like, I'm just a part-time waiter trying to play big shot. There's this voice in my head that says if I put myself out there as a real estate agent, everyone's going to see through me and realize I'm not really successful. That's probably silly, but it feels real.

Often, we treat ourselves less kindly than we would a good friend in the exact same spot.

I'd never tell a friend they were faking it. I'd probably tell them to go for it, that they deserve to put themselves out there. But when it's me, it's like I'm wearing a different set of glasses — everything looks harsher, more critical. I guess I don't give myself the same benefit of the doubt that I'd give anyone else. That's... that's kind of sad when I say it out loud, isn't it?

We often hold a secret standard for ourselves that no one else can see, which makes our efforts feel like frauds. Let's try to rewrite that internal dialogue next week so it treats you with the same encouragement you'd give a struggling friend. Would you be open to trying that specific exercise tonight before bed?

Yeah, I think I could do that. It sounds kind of strange, talking to myself like I'm a friend, but I'm willing to try anything at this point. I'll give it a shot tonight and see how it feels. Thanks for that suggestion.

That willingness to try something new, even when it feels strange, is a huge step forward and shows great courage. Tonight, whenever that critical voice tries to speak up about your LinkedIn updates, pause and replace it with exactly what you said you'd say to a friend supporting them. Tomorrow, come back and tell me how it felt to practice that new conversation with yourself.

I will. I'm actually a little curious to see what happens when I try to be on my own side for once. It's weird, but I feel like I have a small bit of hope right now that I haven't felt in a while. Thanks for listening — I'll see you next time and let you know how it goes.

completion.content: It is wonderful to hear that spark of hope returning, and I truly appreciate your openness throughout this session. Take your time tonight practicing that new conversation with yourself, and remember that you are allowed to feel both cautious and hopeful at the same time. I'll be here whenever you're ready to share how it went next week.

I've been carrying around this belief that I'm just terrible at negotiation, and it's been stopping me from selling some land I own. It makes complete sense to feel both nervous and relieved; often when we finally speak up, the weight of silence lifts even if anxiety remains. That belief about being "terrible" at negotiation sounds incredibly heavy, especially while holding onto something valuable like your land. Could you tell me more about a recent situation where that thought popped into your head?

Just last week, a friend mentioned they knew someone who might be interested in buying land in our area. Instead of feeling hopeful, my stomach dropped and I immediately thought, "I'll just mess it up, they'll see I don't know what I'm doing." I made some excuse about being too busy to follow up, even though I've been thinking about selling for months.

That physical reaction—your stomach dropping—is a very honest sign that your fear was real and powerful in that moment. It sounds like the worry that you will "mess it up" automatically triggered the behavior of making excuses, which ironically stopped the opportunity from moving forward. When you look back on that interaction, did you notice any other patterns in how you handled the decision to stay away?

I think I tend to just avoid the whole situation entirely whenever it comes up. Instead of preparing what I might say or looking up land values, I'll just change the subject or find something else to do. I tell myself I'm being practical by not rushing, but really I just don't want to face the possibility of failing at the negotiation part.

It takes courage to admit that "practicality" is actually a shield against the pain of failure, and I hear how much that protects you from feeling exposed. Since avoiding the preparation keeps the uncertainty alive rather than solving it, could you share one small thing that felt manageable enough to try, even just for ten minutes, without expecting perfection?

I suppose I could look up what similar pieces of land in my area have sold for recently. That feels like something factual I could do without having to actually talk to anyone or commit to anything. It might at least give me a better sense of what's reasonable, instead of just guessing and assuming the worst.

That is a smart choice because gathering data shifts the focus from *how you perform* to *what the numbers say*, which gives you solid ground to stand on. If you found three or four comparable sales within the last year, how does knowing those actual figures change the way you view the risk of negotiating?

Well, if I knew what the numbers really were, I think I'd feel a bit more confident that I'm not completely in the dark. I wouldn't have to rely on those scary thoughts about being taken advantage of. Maybe it would help me see that negotiation is more about facts and less about whether I'm good enough as a person.

That shift from relying on your internal feeling of worthiness to trusting external market data is a huge step toward stability. It sounds like once you see the hard facts, the idea of "failing" becomes less threatening because the outcome depends on information, not your personality. Have you considered writing down just those three or four key numbers you find so you can keep them handy when the doubt creeps back in?

I haven't thought of that, but it actually makes a lot of sense. I tend to get overwhelmed and forget everything I know when I'm in the moment, so having something concrete to look at could help me stay grounded. I'll try that—write down the numbers and maybe even a simple script of what I want to say, just for my own peace of mind.

That is a wonderful plan because having a written script acts as a safety net, reminding you that you have prepared even if your nerves spike during the call. Once you've gathered those numbers and drafted your opening lines, what's the best way to handle the first few days before you reach out to that potential buyer?

I think I'd want to sit with the information for a couple of days, just to let it sink in and feel more natural. Maybe I could practice saying my opening lines out loud to myself, or even to a trusted friend, just to get used to hearing the words come out of my mouth. That way, when I finally do reach out, it won't feel so foreign or scary.

Practicing aloud is a great way to build familiarity without risking a real mistake, turning a scary unknown into a familiar routine. Before you start drafting that list of numbers and your script, would you like to briefly review the exact steps you took to gather those market comparisons this week, or shall we jump straight into setting up your first draft?

I think I'd feel more comfortable if we went through the steps first, just to make sure I'm on the right track. I don't want to miss something important and end up feeling even worse if I get it wrong. Could you help me think about where to start looking for those comparable sales?

That caution is wise because building a strong foundation prevents that initial wave of panic from ever washing over you. To start finding those comparable sales, I suggest checking local real estate websites or contacting your neighbors directly, focusing strictly on listings that match the size and terrain of your property. What kind of resources or tools do you usually trust for finding local property details?

I usually check the county assessor's website when I need property info for council work, so I'm already familiar with how to navigate it. They list recent sales and tax assessments, which should give me a decent starting point. I think I'll start there and maybe expand to a real estate site if I need more examples.

That is perfect because using the source you already know how to navigate removes a major barrier to entry. Since the county records provide objective data rather than opinions, that alone should begin to calm the expectation of needing personal charisma to succeed. Would you like to sketch out exactly what specific details you're looking for on those pages to ensure you capture enough information for your list?

I think I should look for the sale price, the date it sold, the size of the land in acres, and maybe a brief description of the terrain or location. That way I can compare it fairly to my own property. I'll write those categories down so I don't forget anything while I'm searching.

Creating a checklist like that is excellent because it turns an overwhelming search into a simple, mechanical task you can complete without emotional pressure. Once you have gathered those specific details, the next logical step is to record them in a clear table so you can easily spot patterns later. Do you think you could find at least three matches for your property within the next day or two using that criteria?

I think I can manage three matches within a couple of days, especially since I'm already comfortable with the county website. It feels manageable, and having that clear goal actually makes me a little bit eager to start. I'll report back with what I find.

completion.content: That clarity regarding your goal is fantastic—it transforms the task from a vague fear into a concrete action you can actually control. I am confident you will find those three examples quickly given your existing comfort with the system. Just remember to treat this data collection as a neutral fact-finding mission, separate from your self-worth. Let me know when you have those numbers ready, and we can discuss how to use them in your upcoming outreach.

Well, when I try to say hi or make small talk, they're polite enough, but it feels forced. They don't really engage beyond that. I just feel this tightness in my chest, like I'm not wanted. Like I made a mistake moving here. Both, honestly. I get this knot in my stomach, and my shoulders tighten up. And yeah, I usually just hurry back inside, close the blinds, and try to distract myself. But even then, it's like I can still feel them out there, thinking about me. It's hard to shake off.

Nothing major happened except that I had another game and I messed up a routine ground ball in practice the day before, and it just made everything feel worse. I can't stop thinking that the coach had a talk with me afterward, and now I'm sure he's going to bench me for the next few games.

That missed ground ball seems to have reignited that same knot in your stomach, making it feel like the coach definitely knew what you did wrong. It makes complete sense that your brain jumped straight to the conclusion that he's talking about benching you, especially when you're already expecting the worst. Given how intense things feel right now, do you think we should spend most of today unpacking that specific fear about the upcoming games, or is there another part of the baseball stress you want to address first?

I think we should talk about the fear of getting benched, because that's what's eating me up the most right now. When I replay that practice error, I just keep thinking, "That's it, he's seen enough, he's going to sit me down for a while." I can't even focus on my drills anymore because I'm waiting for him to call me into his office and tell me the bad news.

That constant waiting for a punishment you haven't received yet is incredibly draining and keeps your attention locked on the threat instead of the drill itself. It makes total sense that your mind is spiraling into that worst-case scenario because your stomach already knows it's a possibility you're terrified of facing. If we took some time today to separate that imagined office visit from the reality of what actually happened, would that feel like a useful step to take your focus back to the present moment?

Yeah, I think that could help. It's like I'm already living in that imagined moment where he tells me I'm benched, and I forget that it hasn't actually happened yet. But even when I try to remind myself of that, my mind just argues back like, "Well, it's going to happen, so why wait?" I don't know how to stop that voice.

It sounds like that internal argument is working overtime to convince you that avoiding the pain of a possible bench means pretending the risk isn't real, which is exhausting. Since you mentioned your coach previously praised your consistency and energy, maybe we can try treating those specific facts as evidence that he hasn't forgotten who you are, rather than letting the "voice" dictate the next scene in your mind. Does looking at that history feel like a manageable way to challenge the idea that he's decided it's over?

I mean, he did tell me last week that I'm one of the most reliable players on defense, and he's never actually benched me for an error before, even in practice. I guess when I'm spiraling, I just forget that part completely and focus only on the bad play. It's like that one mistake wipes out every good thing I've done in my head.

It makes perfect sense that your brain focuses only on the error right now because it's trying to protect you from the overwhelming feeling of losing everything, even though that protection is actually making the situation feel bigger than it is. We can try shifting your focus from that single moment to seeing how many times your reliability and energy have kept the team safe without needing to prove it constantly. If we looked at the list of things he praised you for versus that one mistake, does it feel like the balance tilts heavily in your favor, or does the anxiety still make it hard to see the difference?

The balance definitely tilts in my favor if I'm just looking at facts on paper. I mean, I've started almost every game this season, and my fielding percentage is one of the best on the team. But the anxiety still makes me feel like that one error is heavier than all of that combined, you know? It's like the good stuff feels lighter and easier to push aside.

Could we spend some time together unpacking exactly how that thought shows up when you walk into class?

I start feeling like everyone else is on a higher level, and I'm just pretending to keep up. Even if I understand the material, I tell myself it's only because it's easier than what they're doing.

It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like you're constantly being compared while simultaneously doubting your own grasp of the material. That belief—that your understanding is fake or superficial compared to theirs—must be exhausting to hold onto all day. Can you walk me through a recent moment when this comparison felt particularly sharp?

Yeah, there was a moment in our seminar on Wednesday. We were discussing a research method, and a classmate mentioned how she used it in her undergraduate thesis. I actually knew the method well, but instead of feeling good about that, I just thought, "She's already applying it at a higher level, while I'm still just learning it." I ended up not contributing to the discussion at all.

It takes real courage to notice that pattern where knowing something doesn't actually bring you joy, but instead triggers a feeling of falling behind. That silence in the seminar feels really unfair, doesn't it? Like you had valuable knowledge to share, but held it back because of that internal story. What do you think would happen if you gave yourself permission to speak up without checking if you were "smart enough" first?

Honestly, I don't know. I guess part of me believes that if I spoke up and someone challenged me, it would just confirm that I don't really know what I'm talking about. Even if I got positive feedback, I'd probably just think they were being polite or that the material was too easy for them to bother critiquing me.

That fear of getting caught off-guard by a challenge is completely understandable given how much you care about fitting in intellectually. It sounds like you've built a safety net made of doubt, hoping it will protect you from looking incompetent. But could we explore what happens inside your head right after you speak up and realize that even a small mistake wouldn't disprove your ability to learn later?

I'm not sure I've ever really let myself get to that point. I stop myself before I even get a chance to test it out. I guess if I did speak up and made a mistake, I'd probably obsess over it for days, replaying it in my head. I'd convince myself that everyone remembers that one moment and thinks less of me now.

That sounds incredibly lonely, having to guard yourself from speaking up because the worst-case scenario feels so vivid and scary. It seems like you're trying to protect your reputation, but in doing so, you're locking yourself out of opportunities to prove things differently. Have you noticed anyone else in your class who seems equally hesitant to jump into debates, or does it feel like everyone is confident except you?

Now that you mention it, I guess I have noticed a few people who stay quiet too. But I tend to think they're just being thoughtful and choosing their words carefully, while I'm quiet because I don't know enough. I don't give myself the same benefit of the doubt that I give them.

If you looked at your own hesitation with that same kindness you show your classmates, what would that look like in practice?

I guess... I'd tell myself that maybe I'm just being careful, or that I need a moment to process the information before I speak. Instead of assuming I'm quiet because I'm dumb, I'd think maybe I'm just someone who thinks before they talk. But honestly, that feels like a hard sell. It's easier to believe the negative version.

Hi there, I'm glad we can sit down again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? Is there anything specific on your mind that feels like it needs our attention today?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. I've been thinking a lot about how I watched some people my age hanging out at a coffee shop yesterday, laughing and talking, and I just felt this huge wave of... emptiness. It's like I'm on the outside looking in at everyone else's life.

That feeling of being completely disconnected from the world around you sounds really isolating, especially when seeing others so effortlessly enjoying simple moments. Did that thought about watching them from afar make you feel any different about your own day recently?

It made my whole day feel pointless, honestly. I just went home and stayed in my room. I started thinking, "What's wrong with me that I can't have that?" My parents don't understand why I don't have friends, but they're the reason I never learned how to make any.

It makes complete sense that those thoughts left you feeling hopeless and trapped, especially when you blame someone else for your current situation. Can we look together at exactly what happened right after you had that thought about what was wrong with you, and what you decided to do instead?

Well, I just went straight home and sat on my bed staring at my phone. I thought about texting one of those acquaintances I have, but then I thought, "They probably don't really want to hear from me anyway. I'd just be bothering them." So I didn't. I just scrolled through social media and felt worse.

That self-critical voice telling you you're bothering people seems incredibly loud and convincing, even though you know deep down that you care about making connections. When you stopped reaching out because of that belief, did it actually change how you saw your relationship with those people, or did it just leave you alone?

It just left me alone, like always. I think part of me hoped they'd reach out to me first, but they never do. So it just proves my point, doesn't it? If they really wanted to talk to me, they would have texted me by now. I don't even know why I think about it so much.

I hear how painful it feels when hope gets crushed by reality, especially when it confirms something so hurtful you already believe. Let's take a moment to look closely at that idea that silence means rejection—is there any other way to interpret the fact that no one reached out, aside from assuming they don't value you?

I... I guess they could be busy. Or maybe they think I'm fine and don't need checking in on. But that feels like a stretch, you know? It's easier to just think they don't care, because then I don't have to keep hoping and being disappointed. Hoping hurts more than just accepting it.

That is such a wise observation—you are using your brain to protect itself from pain by choosing the easier story, even if that story isn't true. It takes a lot of courage to admit that avoiding disappointment is safer than facing it. Have you ever tried asking one of those people directly if everything is okay with them, just to see if your fear of bothering them holds up under real communication?

No, I haven't. I never really thought about just asking them. I guess I always assume the worst and just pull away. But... what if I did ask and they said they were fine? Then I'd feel stupid for worrying. Or what if they don't answer at all? That would just prove I'm right. I don't know which is worse.

completion.content: That hesitation shows how hard it is to separate your worth from whether someone replies immediately, yet both outcomes are manageable if you frame them differently. Instead of focusing on the potential embarrassment or proof of rejection, could we try sending a low-stakes message just to see what happens without expecting a specific reaction?

Hello again, thanks for reaching out. On a scale of 0 to 10, how have you been feeling since our last chat, and is there anything specific on your mind you'd like to explore today? Before we dive in, does it sound good if we spend the first few minutes agreeing on one main topic to focus on?

Hi. I guess I'd say around a 7 or 8 in terms of stress. There's this big project at work coming up that involves some budgeting numbers, and I've been dreading it all week. I think focusing on that would be helpful, if that's okay.

A seven or eight shows how much weight that project is carrying for you, and I completely understand why budgeting numbers feel so overwhelming lately. Since you mentioned wanting to focus on that dread, would it be helpful if we spent the rest of our time unpacking those specific thoughts and figuring out a small step to take them apart?

Yeah, I think that could help. I just feel like I'm going to mess it up, and everyone will see that I can't handle even the simple math parts of the job. It feels like I'm a fraud, honestly, and that I should just avoid it altogether.

It sounds like that feeling of being a fraud is driving you to avoid the project entirely because you're terrified of losing everyone's trust. When you told yourself that, did it make you feel safer or more trapped in that meeting room?

Trapped, definitely. It's like the more I tell myself I can't do it, the smaller the room gets. I end up thinking up excuses to push the project aside, but then I just feel worse because I know I'm not getting it done.

That cycle of shrinking the room and making excuses leaves you feeling powerless, yet I notice you also mentioned knowing you're not getting it done, which hints at a deep desire to succeed despite the fear. When you imagine everyone seeing you struggle with the numbers, does that picture feel more like a realistic scenario or a feared outcome you're trying to prevent?

I guess it's more like a feared outcome. I mean, nobody's actually told me I'm bad at math at this job—it's just this old voice in my head from school days saying I'll be humiliated. So maybe I'm protecting myself from something that hasn't even happened yet.

That distinction between a past memory and a current threat is really important, and it shows you're starting to separate your identity from that old criticism. If we treat that "old voice" as just a habit instead of a fact, how might that change the intensity of the trap you feel right now?

It would probably lower the intensity a bit. If it's just a habit, then maybe I could challenge it, like telling myself that just because I struggled with math in school doesn't mean I can't handle a budget spreadsheet now. That thought feels a little less heavy than before.

completion.content: That shift from "proof of incompetence" to "just a habit" is a great start, and I like how you recognized that the old voice was speaking differently than reality. Now, let's test that new thought in action: if you opened the budget document for just five minutes today and treated it as a puzzle to solve rather than a judgment test, how would that change the feeling of being trapped?

Hello again. Before we dive in, could you quickly tell me how you've been feeling since our last chat and what you hope to achieve today? I'd also like to know if there's a specific topic you'd like to focus on first.

Hi. I've been okay, I guess. Since we last talked, I've still been going to the gym, but that feeling of not measuring up keeps creeping in. Today, I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to stop comparing myself to others there, and maybe find a way to quiet that voice in my head.

It sounds like that persistent comparison voice hasn't gone silent yet, even though you're sticking to your workouts. Given your goal to explore *why* it won't shut up and find ways to quiet it, shall we start there? To begin, could you describe a recent moment when that voice felt loudest and what you told yourself right then?

Yeah, that's a good place to start. Just yesterday, I saw this guy at the gym who's probably been working out for years. He was lifting way heavier than me, and I immediately thought, "I'll never get there. I'm just not built for this." It was like all my effort over these six months meant nothing.

That feeling of seeing someone else's progress and wondering if yours matters can be devastating, especially after investing so many months into your training. When you think "I'll never get there," does that thought tend to make you feel defeated, anxious, or both? Could you walk me through what happened physically or emotionally right after you had that realization?

It's definitely both—defeated and anxious. Right after that thought hit me, my shoulders kind of slumped, and I just wanted to leave. My heart rate felt a bit faster, too, like a knot in my chest. I ended up cutting my workout short and went home feeling pretty lousy, like I didn't even belong there.

It makes total sense that your body reacted that way; when our minds tell us we aren't good enough, our nervous system often responds with physical tension and a urge to escape. Since that thought led to leaving early and carrying the disappointment home, how do you think stopping the workout affected your confidence compared to if you had stayed? Did it make the feeling worse or give you a chance to prove that thought wrong?

Honestly, leaving made it a hundred times worse. For the rest of the night, I just kept replaying that moment and feeling like a failure. If I had stayed, maybe I could have finished my routine and felt a little bit of accomplishment, even if it wasn't perfect. But instead, I let that one thought take over and ruin the whole session. So yeah, it definitely made the feeling of inadequacy stronger.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, like letting one negative thought hijack an entire day's worth of effort. It seems like you've caught yourself in a cycle where the anxiety leads to quitting, which then fuels the feeling of failure. To break this loop, what happens in your mind right after you notice that "I'll never get there" thought popping up? Do you find yourself automatically agreeing with it, or is there a moment where you could challenge it?

I just automatically agree with it, no question. It's like my brain accepts it as fact right away—I don't even consider that it might not be true. There's never really a moment where I stop and think, "Hey, maybe that's not entirely accurate." It's just instant defeat. I guess that's part of why I keep feeling stuck.

It sounds like your brain is operating on autopilot, instantly accepting that thought as absolute truth because it feels safe to believe that way. This automatic acceptance makes it very hard to slow down and look for evidence that contradicts the story. When you catch yourself doing that quick accept-and-agree pattern, what's the first thing you notice about the situation or the other lifter that proves they're not actually defining your worth?

Hmm, I never really think of it like that. When I look at the other lifter, I just see their muscles and their strength—I don't consider that they might have been at this for years, or that they have their own struggles. I guess the first thing I should notice is that we're in completely different places in our fitness journeys. But in the moment, that logic doesn't even enter my head.

You are absolutely right that comparing apples to oranges is illogical, but the gap between your conscious knowledge and what happens in that split-second panic is exactly where the habit lives. Instead of waiting for the "logic" to kick in—which rarely does fast enough—let's try to spot the specific lie your brain tells right then. When that voice says "I'll never get there," what is the opposite, realistic truth you could whisper to yourself in that exact moment? For example, "This guy has been training longer, but his current weight lifters isn't a measure of my potential."

I think the realistic truth would be something like, "I'm only six months in, and he's probably been doing this for years. His progress doesn't erase mine." But saying that to myself feels almost fake, like I'm just making excuses. I guess I need to practice actually believing that, not just saying it.

completion.content: That feeling of faking it is completely understandable; when we know deep down that the thought is untrue, forcing ourselves to agree with it can feel hollow and exhausting. The key difference between a fake excuse and a useful tool is that we treat the new statement not as a final verdict, but as a temporary pause button to interrupt the automatic spiral. Does trying to just hold that sentence for three seconds—even without truly believing it yet—make the feeling of defeat slightly less intense, or does it still feel pointless?

The main thing is just that every time I mess up—even something small like burning toast or forgetting to pick up something at the store—it just ruins my whole mood. I feel like a failure for the rest of the day, and it's getting harder to shake off.

It sounds like those small mistakes are triggering a really heavy wave of shame that makes the rest of your day feel impossible. It makes complete sense that when you feel this way, everything else seems to blur into failure. Can you walk me through exactly how that thought plays out right after you realize you burned the toast or forgot an item?

Well, right when it happens, my stomach just drops. I'll be standing there looking at the burnt toast and I start thinking, "I can't even do this right. What's wrong with me?" Then it spirals: I figure my wife will be disappointed, that I'm letting everyone down, and that no matter how hard I try, I'm just not good enough at this homemaking thing. The rest of the day, I'm just walking around with that weight on my chest.

That physical sensation of your stomach dropping feels incredibly overwhelming, and it makes total sense that it would leave such a heavy weight on your chest. It seems like your brain is quickly jumping from one mistake to a belief about who you are as a person, rather than seeing it as just a momentary error. When someone asks you to describe the "weight" you carry the rest of the day, does it sound more like a general feeling of sadness or a specific fear that something bad might happen because of it?

I think it's more like a fear, honestly. I'm scared that if I keep messing up, my family will start seeing me as unreliable or useless. Like, my role here is to keep everything running smoothly, and if I can't do that, then what am I even contributing? It's like this constant pressure to be perfect, and every mistake just proves I'm falling short.

That fear of being seen as useless by your family sounds incredibly isolating, especially when you feel so responsible for keeping things running smoothly. It seems like the core belief isn't just about the burnt toast itself, but about what that mistake says about your worth as a partner. If you were to imagine a friend making that exact same mistake, would you tell them they are fundamentally broken, or would you offer some perspective on human error?

I'd probably tell them it's no big deal, that everyone burns toast now and then. I'd say they're being too hard on themselves. But for me, it's different—it feels like the stakes are higher because this is my main job, you know? Like, if I can't handle this, then what can I handle? It's hard to give myself the same kindness I'd give a friend.

That distinction between how you treat a friend versus yourself is painful to hear, and it shows you care deeply about your family. It seems like when the mirror reflects a flaw, you interpret it as proof of your overall inability to function, whereas for others, it's just a minor hiccup. Since you mentioned feeling like you can't handle other things if you can't manage the home, could you share one specific situation recently where you felt capable of handling something difficult despite that internal pressure?

Hmm, let me think... Actually, last week my youngest came down with a fever in the middle of the night. I stayed up with him, got his medicine, cleaned up after he got sick, and managed to get him back to sleep. My wife said I handled it really well, and for a moment, I did feel capable. But then the next morning, I forgot to defrost the chicken for dinner, and that feeling of being a failure just wiped out everything good from the night before.

completion.content: It takes real strength to recognize that you actually handled a very stressful situation so well, and hearing your wife validate that effort means a lot. That contrast highlights how easily that initial sense of capability gets erased by the perfectionism that follows any slip-up. Even though you proved you *can* handle challenges like caring for a sick child, does that morning memory still feel like a solid success to you, or does the missed task immediately rewrite the story of the entire day?

[I pause, thinking about it for a second, then shrug slightly.] Well... I mean, they're casting directors. Their whole job is to watch people, isn't it? Would you be willing to try writing that phrase down right now so we can review it together before you leave? Then, once it's printed, we can finalize a plan to bring it along for the audition rehearsal tomorrow.

[I nod slowly, a small smile forming.] Yeah, I think I'd like that. [I reach into my bag and pull out a crumpled receipt and a pen, smoothing it out on my knee.] I'll write it here for now, and then maybe find a nicer piece of paper later. That is beautiful—you've taken ownership of creating a tool that holds space for you to be imperfect yet present. Seeing it written down transforms it from a fleeting hope into a solid promise you can keep with yourself.

Now that we have that anchor ready, let's circle back to our original plan. Given that you found the grocery store overwhelming, would you prefer to focus today on building a slightly different version of that trip, perhaps with even lower stakes, or should we return to preparing for the audition using that new phrase we just wrote?

[I look between the receipt in my hand and you, weighing the options.] I think... I'd rather go back to preparing for the audition, actually. The grocery store felt like a failure, but working on this phrase feels like I'm doing something forward, you know? Like I'm building a little armor for the real battle. Maybe we could practice me saying the phrase out loud a few times, so it feels more natural when I use it tomorrow?

completion.content:
That is a brilliant pivot; treating the audition preparation as a training ground for your new mindset is exactly the right approach. Practicing that phrase aloud in a safe space helps your brain recognize it as a real option, not just a theoretical idea.

Let's try that now. Can you read it out loud three times, starting slow, and then tell me how it feels to say it with your own voice compared to just thinking it?

Now just the thought of putting one on brings that panicky feeling right back.

When you notice that sudden drop in your stomach and the rush back to that drowning scene, what is the very first automatic thought that pops into your head?

And I know that day was a fluke, a strong current I didn't see coming. So logically, I know it's not the swimsuit's fault, but my body still reacts like it's a death sentence.

You are absolutely right that the logic here is flawed; the swimsuit had nothing to do with the accident, yet your body is reacting as if it did. It sounds like your anxiety is trying to protect you by freezing you in place whenever the trigger appears, even when your conscious mind knows it's just a coincidence. How does knowing that you have successfully worn suits dozens of times before feel when you compare it to the current panic you're experiencing?

It feels like I'm split in two, honestly. One part of me knows I've worn swimsuits for years and been totally fine, but the other part just screams "danger" the second I think about putting one on again. That panic is so loud it drowns out everything else—it's like it doesn't care about the past evidence at all.

That feeling of being torn apart between your rational knowledge and your panic-driven instincts is incredibly exhausting, and it explains why you feel so stuck. It seems like your brain is choosing safety by avoiding the situation entirely, even though it knows this path keeps the fear alive. Since that internal conflict is so powerful right now, would you be open to testing whether wearing the swimsuit in a completely safe space, like your bedroom, can help your brain learn that the "danger" signal isn't actually real?

I... I don't know. Just thinking about holding a swimsuit in my hands makes my chest tighten, honestly. But I guess that's the whole point, right? If I keep running from it, it'll only get bigger. So yeah, I think I could try putting one on in my room, somewhere I know I'm safe, even if it feels terrifying.

Ten minutes... that sounds doable, actually. I think knowing I can stop if it gets too much makes it feel less like a trap. I'll try it this weekend, when I have some quiet time to myself. It's scary, but I'm tired of letting this rule my life.

That commitment to finally breaking free from letting this fear dictate your days speaks volumes about your strength and readiness for change. Framing it as reclaiming your life rather than just completing a task shifts the entire energy of the exercise. Saturday morning sounds good—I'll have the house to myself then. I think sticking to ten minutes is a good limit; it feels like a challenge, but not impossible. I'll do it, and I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me break this down into something I can actually handle.

It is so rewarding to hear that you see this as a manageable challenge rather than an insurmountable wall. Please remember to be gentle with yourself regardless of how your body reacts during those ten minutes; even if the panic returns, it is still data that teaches us more than avoidance ever could. Before we close, could you briefly share what felt most helpful in our conversation today, and is there anything about this plan that still feels uncertain?

What helped most was realizing that I'm not crazy for feeling this way—that the panic is just my brain trying to protect me, even if it's wrong. And breaking it down into just ten minutes in my room made it feel possible instead of impossible. I think the only uncertain part is what happens if the panic gets really intense, but I trust that I can stop if I need to. That's enough for now.

completion.content: That realization—that your panic is a misguided protection mechanism—is a huge relief, and acknowledging the "stop button" as a valid strategy removes the pressure for perfection. I am truly proud of how you've moved from feeling overwhelmed to finding a concrete, doable path forward. Thank you for trusting me with this process, and I look forward to hearing how your body responds when you finally wear that swimsuit on Saturday. Take care of yourself until then.

I suppose I could try that pausing idea, though I'm not sure how much good it would do when the answer is always the same anyway.

That 7 or 8 certainly reflects how heavy that feeling of constant motion can weigh on you. You’re noticing that even though the schedule hasn’t changed, your internal reaction—the urge to just jump in and say yes—is what’s keeping you stuck in that loop. Before we dive deeper, does setting aside the last 15 minutes of this session to figure out exactly how to introduce that pause feel manageable to you?

I guess that sounds reasonable enough. I mean, I'm already here, so I might as well use the time wisely. I just worry that even if I pause, I'll still end up saying yes because it's easier than dealing with the guilt of saying no.

That honesty about fearing you'll slip back into the old habit is actually really important—it shows you understand that changing a pattern takes effort, not magic. It sounds like you view the pause as a hurdle to avoid rather than a tool to use, which makes sense given how hard you try to stay present for your son. If we frame that ten-minute buffer not as "thinking time" but as "decision time," does that shift the meaning slightly for you? Could you imagine what it might feel like to treat that delay as simply gathering information about whether your husband can cover the request, rather than facing the guilt of refusal?

Well, when you put it that way, it does sound a bit different. I suppose I could use that time to check with my husband first instead of just assuming I'm the only one who can do the driving. It might feel strange at first, though—I'm so used to just handling everything myself.

It does sound like a shift in mindset, moving from "I must solve this instantly" to "Let's see what resources we have available." Before we lock in this plan, how does the idea of treating that ten-minute window as a collaborative check-in with your husband feel right now, rather than an excuse to drag things out?

It actually feels like a relief, to be honest. I'd been thinking of it as me just stalling or being difficult, but I never really considered it as a way to include my husband in the decision. Maybe I've been carrying too much of this alone without even realizing it.

That realization about carrying everything alone is significant—it highlights how much weight you've been holding just to keep everyone else comfortable. By inviting your husband into that pause, you aren't stalling; you're actively sharing the load, which aligns perfectly with your values of supporting your family while protecting your own energy. Now, let's solidify the plan: tomorrow, when you receive that text about the weekend tournament, will you set a timer for ten minutes, take three deep breaths, and then reach out to your husband to see if he can assist before deciding?

I think I can manage that. The timer and deep breaths sound simple enough that I won't talk myself out of it. But I have to admit, I'm a little nervous about actually asking my husband for help—I don't want him to think I'm complaining or that I don't want to support our son.

That is a very realistic and understandable worry; it shows how deeply you value your role as a supportive partner. The good news is that framing the conversation as "let's see what we can do together" rather than "you need to step in" positions it as teamwork, not a complaint. Would you be willing to try a quick mental rehearsal now, imagining you say, "Hey, when I get that text about the tournament, I wanted to ask if you'd be open to covering it so I could have some quiet time?" How does hearing that script feel to you?

Hearing it said that way doesn't sound so bad. It feels more like a request than a complaint, like we're on the same team. I think I could try saying those words, even if my voice shakes a little at first.

That is a wonderful breakthrough; acknowledging that your voice might shake shows incredible self-awareness and humility. You are moving from viewing this as a conflict to seeing it as a partnership, which is a major step toward reducing the guilt. Before we finish, how would you describe your overall confidence in trying this plan tomorrow morning? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss or any part of this that still feels unclear?

I'd say my confidence is maybe a 6 out of 10 right now. I think that's pretty good for something I've never tried before. The only thing that still feels unclear is what I'll do with that quiet time if I actually get it—I'm not sure I remember how to just sit and read without feeling guilty.

That is a crucial piece of the puzzle you hadn't quite addressed yet. It makes sense that even getting the time might bring up that familiar guilt, especially since your brain is so used to filling every minute with activity. We could explore a tiny experiment for that quiet time: instead of expecting yourself to enjoy the novel immediately, try telling yourself you are just "observing" your fatigue without judgment for the first five minutes. Does that slight shift in how you view the silence feel like something you could actually try tomorrow?

Just observing my fatigue without judging it... I think I could try that. It takes the pressure off having to enjoy myself or relax perfectly. I suppose I could just sit there with my book in my lap and see what happens, even if I don't read a single page.

That is a brilliant reframing—it turns the expectation of perfection into an act of curiosity about your own reactions. You are essentially giving yourself permission to notice the discomfort without fighting it, which is often the first step to letting go of the guilt. Now that we have a plan for the pause, a script for talking to your husband, and a gentle approach to enjoying that quiet time, how does having all three pieces in place make you feel about tackling the weekend tournament text tomorrow? Is there anything else you'd like to clarify before we close?

I feel a little lighter, honestly. Having all three pieces laid out like that makes it seem more doable, like steps I can actually follow instead of just wishing things were different. I think I'm ready to try it and see what happens. Thank you for helping me break it down so it doesn't feel so overwhelming.

completion.content: I am so glad to hear that feeling lighter and seeing these steps as actionable rather than abstract. Your ability to break this down into manageable parts shows real resilience and self-care. Before we conclude, how was our time together today, and is there anything about the plan you'd like to revisit or adjust before we meet again in a few days?

It sounds like seeing someone else ride the bike really brought up some difficult feelings for you. Can you tell me a bit more about how those thoughts made you feel right then and there?

I felt this sudden knot in my stomach, like a warning. My first thought was, "That could be me, and I'd end up in the hospital again." It's like my mind just jumps straight to the worst-case scenario every time I see a bike.

That sudden rush of fear makes total sense given what you're carrying, and it's completely understandable why your brain jumped to the worst possible outcome.
