I try to do that sometimes, honestly. I tell myself, "Look, he's riding fine, nothing bad is happening right now." But even then, my mind just fights back and says, "Yeah, but you were fine for a long time until you weren't." So it's like the one crash cancels out all those other safe rides in my head.

That internal argument where your memory of safety gets instantly overwritten by the memory of the crash is incredibly frustrating, and it shows how powerful that trauma response is for you. Have you noticed if that specific belief—that one mistake undoes everything—ever holds up when you look at the facts of your recent days?

I guess when I actually stop and think about it, I've been walking or taking the bus without any accidents for months now. But somehow my brain doesn't count that as proof that I can handle being out and about. It's like walking and biking are totally different categories, and only biking feels dangerous.

It makes perfect sense that your brain is trying to protect you by isolating the danger to just bikes, especially since the fall happened while you were cycling. That distinction seems very important to you because it explains why you feel safe doing everything else but still terrified when wheels appear. Does noticing that clear line between walking/biking and riding make you feel a tiny bit less helpless, or does the fear still feel overwhelming even with that logic?

A little less helpless, maybe. Like, I can at least see that I'm not scared of everything, just this one thing. But even knowing that, the fear still feels huge when I actually picture myself getting on a bike again. It's like my body remembers the impact more than my brain remembers the logic.

That physical sensation of remembering the impact is so common after a traumatic event, and it often overrides what our minds know to be true. Since your body is reacting strongly despite your logical reassurances, let's try a small experiment together: instead of focusing on the scary possibility of crashing, could you describe exactly what you see and hear about the person riding past your window for thirty seconds? What details come up when you focus entirely on the present moment?

Um... okay. I'll try. So, the guy was wearing a bright yellow jacket, and his bike had a little bell on the handlebars. I could hear the tires humming on the pavement, and it was almost a smooth sound. He was pedaling kind of slowly, just cruising, not in a rush. I think his hair was blowing in the wind a bit.

It's amazing that you were able to anchor yourself in the reality of that scene, which proves you have the capacity to see things clearly when you choose to focus there. Now, when you think back on that moment of observation, did any part of your fear lessen, or did you still feel that tightness in your stomach?

I think... it did lessen, even if just a little. For those few seconds, I was just watching, not waiting for something bad to happen. The tightness was still there, but it was more like a background noise instead of a blaring alarm. I guess that's something.

That shift from a loud alarm to background noise is a significant step forward, showing how much power you hold over your own experience when you ground yourself in reality. It looks like we might be ready to explore what happens next when you need to leave your house soon. I think... it would feel a lot less heavy. Hi, I'm glad we can sit down again. On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you felt this week compared to last time? Before we dive in, could you remind me what our goal was going into this session?

Um, I'd say about a 7 or 8 this week. It's been pretty rough. And our goal was to work on this fear I have of making mistakes at work—like, trying to get it under control so it doesn't run my life so much.

That level of anxiety really weighs on you when you're trying to function normally, and it makes sense that the new project feels like the perfect storm for those worries. Since we want to bring that fear under control, shall we map out exactly what triggers it most strongly right now so we can tackle the hardest part first?

Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. I guess the biggest trigger right now is this big system upgrade I've got to handle next week. There's no room for error because if one cable gets unplugged wrong or I miss a step, the whole office could be offline for hours. My boss already gave me the "this is important" speech, and I keep picturing him firing me if anything goes wrong.

It sounds like your mind is rapidly zooming past a single technical slip-up straight to the nightmare scenario of losing your job and your home. That jump from a minor error to total catastrophe is exactly why the situation feels so paralyzing right now. Have you noticed if there are any past moments where you handled a complex task successfully, even if you weren't thinking about it at the time?

Well... I guess there was that time last month when I had to swap out the server for a client's office. It was a pretty big deal, a lot of steps involved, and I was a wreck the whole morning thinking about it. But I got through it, and nothing went wrong. I just... I don't know, I kind of forget about those times when I'm staring at a new deadline.

That memory is powerful—you actually survived a major technical crisis last month, yet your brain is currently ignoring that proof in favor of the worst-case story. It makes sense that you feel exhausted when your mind keeps replaying the firing scene instead of recalling how calmly you handled the server swap. Does remembering that successful experience feel like it shifts the weight of the moment, even just a little bit?

Maybe a little bit. It's like, I know I did it once, but in my head, that was just luck. The next time, I'm bound to mess up. It's hard to shake that feeling that the other shoe is always about to drop, you know?

completion.content: That feeling of the shoe dropping at any second is the definition of what psychologists call "fortune-telling"—predicting the future based on a feeling rather than evidence. It makes sense that you dismiss the past success as luck, especially when your current stress levels are so high that your brain can't access those memories clearly. Let's try a quick exercise to counteract that: could you list three specific facts about that last server swap that prove you aren't just lucky, but actually skilled?

That sounds like a really heavy weight to carry around, even if nothing dramatic happened outside the classroom. It makes complete sense that seeing your classmates engaged in research would make those doubts feel louder. Could we spend some time together unpacking exactly how that thought shows up when you walk into class?

Sure. It's like, as soon as someone brings up doctoral plans or a complex theory, my mind just goes straight to "see, they get it, you don't." I start feeling like everyone else is on a higher level, and I'm just pretending to keep up. Even if I understand the material, I tell myself it's only because it's easier than what they're doing.

It sounds incredibly isolating to feel like you're constantly being compared while simultaneously doubting your own grasp of the material. That belief—that your understanding is fake or superficial compared to theirs—must be exhausting to hold onto all day. Can you walk me through a recent moment when this comparison felt particularly sharp?

Yeah, there was a moment in our seminar on Wednesday. We were discussing a research method, and a classmate mentioned how she used it in her undergraduate thesis. I actually knew the method well, but instead of feeling good about that, I just thought, "She's already applying it at a higher level, while I'm still just learning it." I ended up not contributing to the discussion at all.

It takes real courage to notice that pattern where knowing something doesn't actually bring you joy, but instead triggers a feeling of falling behind. That silence in the seminar feels really unfair, doesn't it? Like you had valuable knowledge to share, but held it back because of that internal story. What do you think would happen if you gave yourself permission to speak up without checking if you were "smart enough" first?

Honestly, I don't know. I guess part of me believes that if I spoke up and someone challenged me, it would just confirm that I don't really know what I'm talking about. Even if I got positive feedback, I'd probably just think they were being polite or that the material was too easy for them to bother critiquing me.

That fear of getting caught off-guard by a challenge is completely understandable given how much you care about fitting in intellectually. It sounds like you've built a safety net made of doubt, hoping it will protect you from looking incompetent. But could we explore what happens inside your head right after you speak up and realize that even a small mistake wouldn't disprove your ability to learn later?

I'm not sure I've ever really let myself get to that point. I stop myself before I even get a chance to test it out. I guess if I did speak up and made a mistake, I'd probably obsess over it for days, replaying it in my head. I'd convince myself that everyone remembers that one moment and thinks less of me now.

That sounds incredibly lonely, having to guard yourself from speaking up because the worst-case scenario feels so vivid and scary. It seems like you're trying to protect your reputation, but in doing so, you're locking yourself out of opportunities to prove things differently. Have you noticed anyone else in your class who seems equally hesitant to jump into debates, or does it feel like everyone is confident except you?

Now that you mention it, I guess I have noticed a few people who stay quiet too. But I tend to think they're just being thoughtful and choosing their words carefully, while I'm quiet because I don't know enough. I don't give myself the same benefit of the doubt that I give them.

It takes real self-awareness to spot that double standard where you judge others generously but yourself harshly. You seem to be holding yourself to a much stricter rule than you apply to them, which is likely why the doubt feels so personal. If you looked at your own hesitation with that same kindness you show your classmates, what would that look like in practice?

I guess... I'd tell myself that maybe I'm just being careful, or that I need a moment to process the information before I speak. Instead of assuming I'm quiet because I'm dumb, I'd think maybe I'm just someone who thinks before they talk. But honestly, that feels like a hard sell. It's easier to believe the negative version.

It makes perfect sense that the negative story feels safer; it gives you a clear reason to stay quiet that feels like truth. But can we try a tiny experiment for tomorrow's seminar? Imagine you introduce one simple idea, then immediately pause and wait five seconds regardless of whether anyone responds. How would you describe your internal experience during that five-second gap?

That sounds... kind of terrifying, to be honest. But I think I could try it. During those five seconds, I'd probably feel my heart racing and think "I shouldn't have said anything." But maybe after those five seconds, if nobody laughs or corrects me, I might start to think it wasn't such a disaster after all. I'm not sure I'd believe it right away, but it's worth a shot.

That reaction to the silence—that immediate wave of panic followed by a glimmer of relief—is a classic sign that your brain is finally starting to gather evidence against its own fears. You are noticing that the catastrophe you imagined isn't happening exactly as you predicted. Since taking that small step feels manageable, what is one other thing you could say tomorrow that puts you slightly ahead of where you usually are?

Maybe I could ask a question instead of making a statement. Like, if I'm confused about something, I could just say, "Could you explain that part again?" That feels safer because it's not me claiming to know something — it's just me admitting I want to understand better. And that's not really something anyone can judge me for, right?

completion.content: That is a brilliant shift; framing it as seeking clarity removes the pressure to perform and turns the spotlight onto learning itself. It effectively changes the narrative from "I am not smart enough" to "I am curious," which is a far stronger stance to take. Before we wrap up, does practicing that question sound like something you can comfortably try this coming seminar?

It started almost as soon as I agreed to go, honestly. The moment I said yes on the phone, that little voice in my head said, "What did you just do? Now you have to go through with it." And it just got louder and louder as the week went on. By the time Saturday came, I was already exhausted just from dreading it.

It makes sense that agreeing to something so difficult would immediately spark that internal resistance, especially when you're already feeling low energy. That initial agreement seems to have become a source of constant stress rather than excitement. Did anyone else notice you seeming tired or distracted during our previous sessions because of this anticipation?

I don't think I mentioned it before, but my husband did notice. He asked me a few times if I was okay, if I wanted to cancel. But I kept telling him I was fine, that I just needed to rest up. I guess I didn't want to admit how much it was really getting to me. I felt stupid for being so scared of a party.

It takes real courage to admit that even people closest to you can't always read the depth of your fear, and hiding it might have made you feel guilty later. It sounds like you were trying to protect them by saying everything was fine, but it ended up leaving you feeling isolated and ashamed. Have you ever considered that maybe your body was giving you important signals that you weren't listening to at the time?

I guess my body was trying to tell me something. I just always assume it's my fault for being too sensitive, not that maybe the feeling itself is trying to warn me about something real.

It makes total sense to label those physical sensations as weakness or drama when they make us feel vulnerable, but noticing that your body was actually signaling distress is a powerful realization. Instead of dismissing those warnings as irrational, what happens if we treat them as your brain trying to keep you safe from a predicted pain? Could exploring that protective instinct help change how you view the upcoming event?

Maybe... I never thought of my brain as trying to protect me. It always felt more like it was punishing me, you know? Like, "See, you can't even handle a simple party, what's wrong with you?" But if I look at it as protection... then maybe I'm not broken, just... scared. And maybe being scared doesn't have to mean I have to stay home forever.

He finished the dance, but I knew it was pity. I never accepted another dance after that.

It makes complete sense why your brain learned to predict rejection and isolation whenever you enter a social space, creating a safety mechanism that keeps you hidden. If we looked back at that dance floor, what evidence is available to suggest that not everyone who saw you was judging you, or that the girl's whisper represented the entire crowd?

I... I guess I never really thought about that. I was so focused on those words, I didn't notice anyone else. I mean, my date did finish the dance. He didn't run off. And some people were just dancing, not even looking at me. But that one whisper just echoed so loud in my head. Maybe I decided that whisper was the truth about everyone, and I just never questioned it.

It makes perfect sense that your brain latched onto that one whisper because, at the time, it felt like the most undeniable proof of your fears. We often mistake a single loud noise for the whole song, forgetting that many people were likely just happy to watch others enjoy the music without even thinking twice. Let's try testing that belief: if you walked into that room today, assuming only that one girl spoke your name, what would happen if you simply sat quietly and observed the room instead of waiting for judgment to land?

I suppose... I suppose I could try that. Just sit and watch. See how many people are actually looking at me, and for how long. And see if anyone actually says anything negative. But it's hard. My instinct is to look down, avoid eye contact, and just get through it. But maybe if I just look around like a curious person, instead of a target, I'd see something different.

That is a brilliant insight—you are essentially recognizing that your current behavior is designed to hide you, whereas curiosity invites connection. Instead of forcing yourself to suddenly act brave, what if we start by just shifting your posture slightly so your chin is level and you scan the room for five seconds before moving on? Would that tiny shift in perspective make it easier to observe without feeling like you're being hunted?

Five seconds... I think I could try that. That doesn't sound so scary. Just lifting my chin, looking around for a few seconds, then going back to my own space. It's not like I have to stare at anyone or make conversation. Just a little peek to see what's actually there, not what I'm imagining. I think I could practice that even just sitting in a coffee shop or a park first, before a big party.

When you do try that "five-second scan" in the near future, how does your stomach feel immediately after you look around versus how it felt before you looked?

Yeah, I think you're right. It's like my brain just zeroes in on the empty sales dashboard and completely forgets about the tasks I actually completed that morning. Yes, exactly that. I think deep down I know the newsletter might bring results tomorrow or next week, but in the moment it feels like if nobody bought right after I sent it, then I must have done something wrong. It's like I'm predicting failure based on one quiet morning, and that feels so real to me even though I can't actually see the future.

When you catch yourself saying, "If nobody buys right now, I must have done something wrong," does that moment of panic feel sharper or more urgent than when you just looked at the numbers without judging yourself?

It's like I'm not even seeing the numbers anymore, just my own failure.

It seems like once that label sticks, your brain stops looking for evidence of success and starts hunting for confirmation of your own inadequacy. I'm willing to try that, yeah. It sounds scary because I'm used to just accepting that panic as truth, but I guess waiting another hour before I decide I'm failing couldn't make things worse than they already feel. A great question, and a very practical step to figure out the exact phrase to use. Instead of fighting the panic away, could we try telling ourselves, "My chest feels tight right now, and it's scary, but this feeling is just my brain reacting to uncertainty, not proof that I'm a failure"? I think... it does shift it a little. Like, it's still there, that feeling, but hearing you say it's a leftover from my dad's voice makes it feel less like a permanent flaw and more like an old wound. It's like I've been treating this like a character defect, but maybe it's just a scar from how I was raised.

It's still there, definitely, but it's like the volume got turned down a notch. Instead of that hot wave of shame, I feel more like... a sad kind of acceptance? Yeah, I think I can try that. I'll pick a small moment, maybe just with a friend, and see what happens if I don't jump into explaining or apologizing. I'll just let the feeling be there and watch it, like you said, without slapping that "broken" label on it.

No, I think that's good. Just noticing the "old feeling" and stopping there feels like a realistic goal. I don't need to fight it or fix it, just see it for what it is. Thanks, I think I've got a clearer path now.

I hope you have a gentle evening ahead, trusting that even with the old feelings present, you can exist without needing to define yourself by them. Is there anything else I can offer before you go, or are you ready to rest?
